Since quantitative regression requires a unique DLS-derived hydrodynamic diameter, the regression model is restricted to monomodal DLS distributions, while a complementary classification model identifies synthesis conditions for which quantitative prediction is applicable. Using equivalent out-of-sample validation (OOB and LOOCV), the ML and DoE models showed comparable generalization (MAE = 40.92 and 40.46 nm, respectively). The final ensemble model achieved an R2 of 0.74, an MAE of 23.81 nm, compared to an R2 of 0.60, an MAE of 33.54 nm for the DoE model, while retaining the complete synthesis parameter space, making it better suited for synthesis guidance. Additionally, classification models using both random forests and large language models (LLMs) are evaluated to distinguish between large and small particles. These classification models exhibited only modest predictive performance, indicating that this small data set is insufficient to fully exploit the capabilities of complex LLMs. Overall, this study demonstrates that carefully curated small data sets, paired with robust classical ML, can effectively support the synthesis of Cu NPs and highlights that for lab-scale studies, complex models like LLMs may offer limited benefits. The validation experiments further indicate the potential of ML guided synthesis to improve the efficiency of experimental optimization and reduce resource consumption.

Prefilled syringes (PFS) have undergone a paradigm shift, transitioning from passive primary container closure systems into complex, integrated drug-device combination products designed for modern biopharmaceuticals. Their ready-to-administer presentation streamlines clinical workflows, ensures rigorous dosing precision, minimizes contamination risks, and facilitates patient-centric home self-administration. The rapid proliferation of therapeutic monoclonal antibodies, recombinant proteins, peptides, and high concentration subcutaneous formulations has underscored the vital importance of container contact materials, silicone lubrication dynamics, needle geometry, and mechanical device integration. Contemporary PFS platforms encompass traditional Type I borosilicate glass, cyclic olefin polymer (COP), cyclic olefin copolymer (COC), and specialized silicone-reduced or silicone-free platforms. Each material matrix presents a distinct trade-off regarding gas/moisture barrier properties, fracture resistance, dimensional tolerances, extractables (E&L) profiles, and interface-induced drug degradation. For biological macromolecules, drug-container compatibility represents a critical quality attribute (CQA); protein adsorption and interfacial denaturation at glass, polymer, elastomer, air-liquid, and silicone-oil interfaces frequently induce subvisible particle generation and irreversible aggregation. Silicone oil microdroplets remain a focal technical challenge due to potential migration and nucleation effects, while residual manufacturing contaminants such as tungsten species can induce localized protein unfolding. Concurrently, injectability functionality is paramount for viscous high-concentration biologics, were hydraulic resistance and extrusion dynamics scale critically with needle lumen diameter and fluid rheology. This review provides a comprehensive review covering component architecture, material interaction pathways, silicone dynamics, fluid mechanical modelling, clinical human factors, regulatory frameworks, and next-generation smart delivery devices Keywords: Prefilled syringe; Drug-device combination system; Primary container closure; Biologics stability; Monoclonal antibodies; Silicone oil migration; Cyclic olefin polymer (COP); Injectability mechanics; Autoinjectors; Extractables and Leachables (E&L)

Introduction. Climate change has important implications for human health. Temperatures continue to rise and extreme weather conditions become more frequent. Resulting changes in ecosystems will impact health in general and more specifically, distribution of communicable, vector-borne and heat-related diseases. It is imperative to adopt proactive measures to anticipate and mitigate the health impact of climate change. New sensors, skills and tools are required to predict impact on human health and conceptualise proactive measures against adverse consequences of rising temperatures. Materials and methods. A search of the current literature on anticipatory research specific to sensors, skills and tools for prediction was employed. A design thinking model, the ClimateSense Model was conceptualised based on the analysis. Results. Sensors include physical sensors and information technology such as remote sensing with satellites, aircrafts and drones, biological sensors like RNA and DNA sequencing technologies, and chemical sensors for greenhouse gases. Tools include mobile applications and artificial intelligence, internet-of-things technology, and crowdsourcing. Skills involve digital skills to interpret and communicate sensor-derived data using interactive maps, plots, time series, and analysis of big data with statistical skills or artificial intelligence. Conclusion. Synergistic combination of tools, skills and sensors, as conceptualised in the ClimateSense model, are essential to anticipate consequences of climate change for health. By promoting anticipatory preparedness, policymakers, healthcare professionals and communities can better mitigate the adverse health impacts of climate change, build resilience to its effects and define a planetary health strategy. Key messages. Climate change significantly impacts human health through rising temperatures and ecosystem changes. New sensors, tools, and skills are essential to predict and mitigate health consequences of climate change. The ClimateSense model promotes proactive strategies to enhance preparedness and resilience against climate-related health risks.

Background: Due to prolonged slouching and biomechanical overload from feeding, this becomes common among breastfeeding moms. This posture can bring about scapular dyskinesis like the SICK scapular syndrome.Objective: To determine the prevalence and patterns of shoulder pain and functional disability associated with scapular dyskinesis among lactating mothers.Methods:A cross sectional observational study of 100 lactating mothers in the age group of 20-40 years was conducted to assess shoulder pain and disability by pain scoring using visual analogue scale (VAS), disability scoring by shoulder pain and disability index (SPADI), and to screen for scapular dyskinesia using lateral scapular slide test (LSST). Statistical analysis was done using SPSS software 25.0.Result: Most participants reported Bilateral (68%) symptoms compared to the unilateral scapular Involvement (32%) mainly involving dominant side. According to SPADI 37% had moderate pain, 5% had light pain, and 58% had severe pain. The most problematic functional limitations were those which involve pushing the affected limb (47% moderate, 21% severe), to reach for something (48% moderate, 24% severe) and to carry anything (67% had considerable problems). Only those concerning the wearing of shirts and pants where more than 75% of mothers had only few problems. A statistically significant positive association was found between the duration of lactation and the age of the mothers (r=0.567; p<0.01) with greater pain to the shoulders.Conclusion: Early ergonomic support and physiotherapy might have a key role in symptoms management and to reduce further long-term problems of musculoskeletal nature. The results indicate a significant presence of SICK scapular Syndrome and Shoulder pain in lactating Mothers particularly among those having prolonged periods of Breast feeding.

This protocol describes a scoping review that will identify, map, and synthesize the outcomes and measurement tools used in empirical research on manuscript peer review, providing the initial evidence base for the Primary Evaluation outcomEs for Research on peer review - A Core Outcome Set (PEER-COS). Guided by JBI methodology and the COMET Handbook and COS-STAD principles, the review will search seven bibliographic databases, preprint servers, and 69 grey-literature sources for eligible English-language systematic reviews, experimental, quasi-experimental, and observational studies published from 1986 onwards. Eligible studies must evaluate an empirically measured outcome related to peer review of scholarly manuscripts, including, for example, quality, timeliness, transparency, fairness, reliability, or stakeholder experience. Screening and data extraction will be supported by the otto-SR artificial-intelligence platform and subject to predefined human quality checks; identified outcomes will be synthesized quantitatively and thematically into unique outcome concepts and broader domains. The resulting candidate outcome list will inform a three-round international Delphi consensus process involving relevant interest holders—including researchers, editors, peer reviewers, funders, statisticians, and patient and public partners—to establish a core outcome set for future research evaluating manuscript peer review and peer-review interventions.

Proactive bug discovery is an important software-engineering problem. Even though coding agents are already widely deployed in this domain, their capabilities remain understudied. In particular, the challenging task of finding all bugs that human maintainers would repair across an entire repository has not been studied yet. To close this gap, we introduce PROBE, a benchmark consisting of all 2,457 bugs fixed over the course of 18 months across 20 diverse GitHub repositories, together with a method for matching candidate findings to this partial reference set. We evaluate coding agents across frontier models and find they all achieve a recall of below $21\%$ and a precision of less than $9\%$ with respect to the reference set. While stronger models increase recall substantially from $8\%$ to $17\%$, they do not improve precision. Surprisingly, despite the low precision, LLM and human evaluators still judge $85\%$ of findings valid. Crucially, we find that found bug distributions are similar across agents but differ substantially from those of bugs fixed by maintainers. The practical relevance of bug discovery and the low recall of frontier models make this benchmark a valuable resource for both model users and developers.

The article is devoted to the problem of detecting faulty conditions and cases of improper maintenance of automatic fire detection and public alert systems. The aim of the work is to systematize the causes of failures and false alarms, as well as to analyze the regulatory legal risk indicators that allow supervisory authorities to identify potentially hazardous facilities. The study provides a detailed classification of the causes of false alarms, distinguishing four key groups: technical malfunctions, violations of operating conditions, environmental influences and the human factor. The risk indicators approved by Order of EMERCOM of Russia № 364 are analyzed, and the impact of electrical faults (overload, short circuit, high contact resistance) on the operability of system components is considered. Based on the provisions of GOST R 59638-2021 and GOST R 59639-2021, practical recommendations are formulated for ensuring operational reliability at the stages of design, commissioning and maintenance. The novelty of the work lies in the comprehensive linking of the risk indicators used by supervisory authorities with specific physical equipment defects and organizational maintenance errors.

CAPTCHAs and bot detection have helped protect Web services from automated abuse for decades by distinguishing humans from bots. However, the emergence of LLM-powered agents introduces a new setting: Web services increasingly accommodate agents as legitimate users. Without a way to distinguish agents from other automated clients such as simple bots and scripts, these services risk large-scale automated junk submissions that waste service resources and consume users' attention or tokens. In this paper, we investigate a novel question for today's Web: "How can a Web service obtain evidence that a client is an agent?" We introduce the concept of "Proof-of-Agentness" (PoA), a mechanism for distinguishing agents from other automated clients, motivated by the parallel between human attention and an agent's inference resources. We outline two approaches: active verification through challenge-response and passive analysis of service-visible signals. Eight language models achieve an overall accuracy of 96.5% on our challenges, with an average overhead of 1,647 tokens. For passive analysis, we conduct an IRB-approved user study comparing the Web interactions of twelve human participants and representative Bot and Agent implementations, achieving an average classification accuracy of 95.8% across four classifiers, motivating further study.
topics: Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

documents.abstract: In unavoidable crash scenarios, vehicles may have to allocate harm between occupants and pedestrians, raising a central question for autonomous vehicle ethics: should they prioritize occupant protection or minimize overall casualties? This study examines public acceptance of casualty-minimizing stay and occupant-protective swerve maneuvers in moral dilemmas involving human-driven vehicles (HDVs) and autonomous vehicles (AVs), with one occupant and one to five pedestrians. Based on data from Chinese participants (N = 1,188), the results show that participants generally accepted occupant sacrifice when it spared multiple pedestrians, and that acceptance of casualty minimization increased as pedestrian numbers increased. However, the same stay maneuver received lower acceptance when performed by an AV than by an HDV, especially in the one-occupant-versus-one-pedestrian scenario. These findings extend AV ethics research beyond forced-choice preferences by showing how people evaluate concrete vehicle maneuvers, and offer empirical evidence for designing and governing ethical decision rules in unavoidable crash scenarios.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

documents.abstract: Accurate quantitative mapping of gamma-ray emitters is critical for applications ranging from radiological emergency response and environmental monitoring to nuclear security and deep space exploration. Here, we show that such mapping can be achieved by combining mobile gamma-ray spectrometry with high-fidelity Monte Carlo simulations and full-spectrum Bayesian inference. Using 6 s of single-pass mobile spectrometry data benchmarked against independent in-situ and laboratory assays, we demonstrate decisive source mixture identification (>5σ), meter-scale source localization, and recovery of source activities with percent-level accuracy. The developed method marks a critical advance in quantitative gamma-ray sensing, enabling improved radiological situational awareness, enhanced terrestrial geophysical and geochemical mapping, as well as more robust constraints on radionuclide abundances on extraterrestrial bodies across the Solar System.

Chest radiography is the most widely performed imaging examination worldwide and serves as a first-line test across emergency, inpatient and outpatient care. Its interpretation is nevertheless demanding, and diagnostic errors, including missed pneumonia, pulmonary nodules and pleural effusions, are frequent even among experienced readers [1]. Rising imaging volumes and radiologist workforce constraints have accelerated interest in artificial intelligence (AI) decision support, and by 2022 about 190 radiologic AI programs had received approval from the United States Food and Drug Administration, with approvals increasing each year [2,3]. Controlled reader studies show that AI assistance can improve performance when the algorithm is accurate. In a retrospective multireader multicase study, the macro-averaged area under the curve (AUC) of radiologists across 127 chest radiograph findings rose from 0.713 unaided to 0.808 with AI assistance [4]. Another reader study reported higher AUROCs for pneumothorax (0.885 to 0.969) and nodules (0.724 to 0.752), together with a roughly 10% reduction in reporting time [5]. These results have supported the view that AI will help readers by default. AI output is, however, never perfectly accurate. A review of 503 algorithm studies, cited in recent human-factors work in radiology, reported pooled sensitivity of 0.87 and specificity of 0.89 for chest radiograph abnormalities, implying that about 13 of 100 abnormal examinations and 11 of 100 normal examinations would receive an erroneous output [6]. The clinical value of AI therefore depends not only on algorithm accuracy but also on how readers respond when the algorithm is wrong.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Implicit misogyny often requires background knowledge to be understood. To address this challenge, we propose a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework for detecting and explaining implicit misogyny in English and Italian, leveraging encyclopedic, slang and feminist knowledge sources. Using the ImplicIT-Mis and SBIC+ datasets, we evaluate the contribution of each knowledge source to detection and explanation quality, investigating also whether RAG addresses known LLM failure modes in implicit misogyny. Results show that RAG improves recall on ImplicIT-Mis, but does not improve detection performance on SBIC+. However, human evaluation shows that RAG-based explanations are preferred over no-RAG explanations in both languages. Feminist literature emerges as the most consistently useful source for detection and explanation.

Ranking functions are a fundamental technique for proving loop termination, but constructing them manually is challenging and requires substantial expertise. We propose RAINFALL, a neuro-symbolic framework which follows the generate-verify-refine paradigm and tightly integrates LLMs with symbolic verification. RAINFALL formulates ranking function synthesis as a code-completion task by inserting placeholders into the input program and constraining the LLM to fill four predefined slots for each loop. The completed program is then checked by a symbolic verifier. If verification succeeds, a valid ranking function is obtained; otherwise, the verifier's diagnostics are translated into natural-language feedback that guides iterative refinement of the LLM's output. We evaluate RAINFALL on two public benchmark suites comprising 358 terminating C programs. Using MiniMax V2.7, RAINFALL synthesizes verifiable ranking functions for 323 programs (90.22%), outperforming all promising baselines. In particular, it solves 12 more programs than PROTON 2.1, the best-performing baseline and winner of the SV-COMP 2026 Termination category. Furthermore, combining RAINFALL with PROTON 2.1 increases the success rate to 96.65% (346/358 programs). We also conduct ablation study confirming individual contributions of placeholder contracts, few-shot examples, symbolic verification, and diagnostic information feedback. Experiments across LLMs further confirm the effectiveness of RAINFALL. Our results suggest a generic, sound framework for ranking-function synthesis and, beyond termination, LLM-assisted synthesis of formally checkable liveness certificates, both of which represent new directions of software engineering research.

Background and Aims Patient education materials (PEMs) support patient understanding and engagement in care. This study evaluated the readability, understandability and actionability of non-oncological urological PEMs produced by the British Association of Urological Surgeons (BAUS) and the European Association of Urology (EAU), and explored agreement between human and AI-assisted PEMAT-P assessment. Methods and Results A cross-sectional descriptive analysis assessed eight matched PEMs relating to urinary tract infection, urinary incontinence, benign prostatic enlargement/lower urinary tract symptoms, and nocturnal polyuria. Readability was assessed using Flesch Reading Ease (FRE), Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL), Simple Measure of Gobbledygook (SMOG), and Gunning Fog Index. Understandability and actionability were assessed using the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT-P). Mean FKGL was 11.85 ± 2.77, SMOG 13.24 ± 2.39, Gunning Fog 14.09 ± 3.22, and FRE 48.5 ± 13.32. All materials exceeded the recommended reading level. Mean PEMAT-P understandability and actionability were 91.0% and 88.3%. Human–AI item-level agreement for understandability and actionability was 83.6% and 81.8%; Cohen's κ was 0.25 and 0.23, and Gwet's AC1 was 0.79 and 0.76. Conclusion The materials exceeded recommended reading levels despite variable PEMAT-P scores. Human vs AI differences remained, requiring further evaluation of PEMs to establish the potential role of AI as an adjunct to human PEMAT-P assessment.

This study examines the extent to which generative artificial intelligence aligns with human experts in the visual assessment of urban open spaces. Site quality is addressed across five dimensions: spatial accessibility and organization; usage and social function; environmental quality and comfort; safety and inclusivity; and perceptual and aesthetic quality. The same images, indicators, and five-point scale regarding three heavily used public open spaces in Rize city center were evaluated by 20 architects and landscape architects, as well as by ChatGPT and Gemini. The comparison revealed that the level of agreement between the AI and the experts varied depending on the specific site and quality dimension. While alignment was high regarding features that are directly observable—both physically and visually—differences became more pronounced regarding perceptual and aesthetic qualities. The findings suggest that AI can serve as a complementary tool to support visual assessment rather than a replacement for human expertise.

Real-Time Hand Gesture Recognition (HGR) has emerged as a key model of modern Human Computer Interaction (HCI) technologies, enabling touchless and intuitive interactive experiences for a wide range of HCI applications, from assistive technology, virtual and augmented reality to industrial production lines. Although AI and DL open up important opportunities, there are practical challenges to developing and deploying real-time HGR systems that are strong to issues such as computational complexity, variations in the environment, and latency. This survey reviews the state-of-the-art in real-time HGR, including recent work in and algorithmic approaches for various sensor modalities and different stages of the processing pipeline, including detection, tracking, and spatial-temporal classification, using monocular RGB cameras and multi-modal depth sensing systems. In addition, we cover applications such as sign language recognition, healthcare hygiene systems, automotive user interfaces, and human-robot collaboration (HRC), and challenges such as occlusion invariance, light variability, performance versus portability trade-offs, constraints imposed by edge-device deployment, and potential research avenues for multimodal artificial intelligence systems of the future.

PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Advances in multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnosis and treatment have altered disease trajectories, yet many people with MS (pwMS) continue to experience complex symptom burden, functional limitations, and reduced quality of life (QoL). This review summarizes recent developments in neurorehabilitation, focusing on screening and assessment, intervention delivery, and outcome or impact evaluation across symptoms and disability domains. RECENT FINDINGS: Research evidence supports routine, multidimensional screening that goes beyond assessing symptom severity to capture functional limitations, participation restrictions, and social determinants of health (SDoH). Digital technologies, including wearables, remote monitoring, and artificial intelligence-assisted assessments, offer opportunities for more ecologically valid and accessible evaluation, although usability, digital exclusion, and implementation issues remain. Neurorehabilitation is increasingly viewed as a treatment that should begin early in the disease course rather than being reserved for advanced disability. Exercise interventions, cognitive rehabilitation, psychological therapies, vocational rehabilitation, and integrated multidisciplinary approaches demonstrate benefits across physical, cognitive, emotional, fatigue, and QoL outcomes. Telerehabilitation and technology-supported interventions, including virtual reality, exergaming, and neuromodulation, show promise in improving access and outcomes, but more research is needed. To sustain long-term neurorehabilitation benefits, teaching self-management strategies and brain-health behaviours may be beneficial. SUMMARY: Neurorehabilitation is a core component of comprehensive MS care, complementing pharmacological treatment. Evidence favours early, personalized, function-focused interventions delivered through flexible, tiered, and multidisciplinary models. Research gaps include implementation of screening pathways, optimization of person-to-treatment matching and dosing, integration of SDoH, development of meaningful patient-centred outcomes, evaluation of cost-effectiveness, and improved equity of access to rehabilitation services and research across diverse populations.

Abstract Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive and heterogeneous breast cancer subtype for which artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated across diagnostic, prognostic, and treatment response applications. This study presents a comparative bibliometric analysis of AI-related TNBC research indexed in Scopus (n=1,037), Web of Science (n=557), and PubMed (n=763) from 2013-2026. Publication trends, citation impact, leading contributors, international collaboration, knowledge structure, and thematic evolution were examined using database-appropriate bibliometric and network analyses. Using complete year data through 2025, publication output showed statistically significant increasing trends across all three databases, with 2020-2025 compound annual growth rates of 50.13% for Scopus, 49.78% for Web of Science, and 42.84% for PubMed. The United States emerged as the dominant international collaboration hub, while collaboration between the United States and China formed the strongest bilateral link. Thematic evolution showed an early emphasis on machine learning, followed by expansion of deep learning and radiomics and, more recently, parallel imaging/computational and clinical/biological themes involving MRI, treatment response prediction, the tumor microenvironment, immunotherapy, and precision medicine. Scopus co-citation and bibliographic coupling analyses further identified established intellectual foundations and contemporary research fronts. Overall, AI-TNBC research is expanding rapidly, while data heterogeneity, external validation, interpretability, and clinical translation remain important challenges.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence in primary education is changing the way teaching materials are structured, information is acquired, and learning decisions are made. These changes require a reconsideration of the teacher's position, particularly when system recommendations begin to influence assessments of children's needs and abilities. This article aims to redefine the role of primary school teachers through the relationship between pedagogical agency, knowledge authority, and educational ethics. The review employs a critical narrative literature approach to 19 selected publications from 2021–2026, encompassing empirical research, research reviews, conceptual articles, and policy documents that provide open access or official download facilities. The literature is reviewed based on educational context, type of evidence, conceptual contributions, and limitations of its application to primary schools. The synthesis shows that the benefits of AI depend on learning objectives, professional judgment capacity, and institutional support. Teacher agency requires the authority to review, modify, and reject system recommendations. Knowledge authority rests on the ability to explain the basis for a claim and guide the examination of evidence. Educational ethics need to be embodied in data protection, equitable access, child engagement, and the sharing of responsibilities. The article proposes the role of teachers as learning designers, knowledge assessors, relational facilitators, and advocates for children's interests. This reconceptualization requires case-based professional development and school governance that does not center all technological risks on teachers.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Embodied foundation models have expanded robot capabilities, but autonomous execution does not automatically provide autonomous improvement. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) concerns retained changes that can influence subsequent improvement, including the stronger case in which an agent revises the procedures that generate and evaluate future updates. This survey connects large-model learning and reasoning, agent memory and skills, and RSI theory. We compare general agent harnesses with embodied harnesses and organize the literature along four axes: improvement targets, update mechanisms, decision authority and evidence conditions. The method review covers reflection and knowledge revision, executable programs and harness evolution, adaptive experience acquisition, parameter learning, world-model revision, and cross-layer selection and meta-improvement. We analyze how large models guide interventions across these components and distinguish execution correction, persistent capability improvement and revision of the improver. Long-horizon tasks and physical priors are examined as complementary considerations for memory, execution, world modeling and evaluation within this broader framework. We compare representative methods and review benchmarks, datasets, development partitions and resource accounting. Existing evidence supports several forms of retained improvement, while comparable evidence for improved improvement procedures remains limited. Open problems include causal failure attribution, reliable feedback, safe inheritance, competence preservation, model validity, transferable improvers and principled stopping decisions.

Interactive technology is increasingly built for speed, and generative AI now answers before a question is fully formed. Yet the capacity to pause, interpret and decide for oneself is central to wellbeing, learning and meaningful use. HCI has named paradigms for sensing emotion, changing behavior, calming attention and tracking the self. However, none of them takes human reflection, and the slowing down it requires, as its organizing aim. This article defines that paradigm, reflective computing, and derives it from what thirty years of designs lack. We analyzed 134 interactive systems from 17 ACM venues (1996-2026) in two phases. First, an abductive gap analysis read every system against reflection theory, and seven recurring gaps defined seven dimensions, namely tempo agency, invitational form, interpretive openness, reflective depth, temporal span, protected idleness and ethical non-extraction. Second, two independent coders scored every system with a codebook (Krippendorff's alpha 0.67 to 0.84 for five dimensions; ICC 0.82 for the overall score). The system sets the pace in 51 designs, 74 support only momentary use, only 12 scaffold reflection beyond description, and 56 papers are silent on the inner states they collect. No system expresses all seven dimensions strongly, and only 20 meet the definition. Slow and experience centered design comes closest, whereas persuasive technology and human-AI interaction score lowest. Factor and latent class analyses reveal two cultures of reflection, one working through form and the other through scaffolded thought, which only one system combines. Systems that let people set the pace score markedly higher, even with paradigm and form controlled (odds ratio 13.5). Hence, reflective computing is proposed as a paradigm whose aim is a human capacity rather than a system function, and which treats slowness as valuable only when people choose it.

Aeon Mundi is a collection of adaptive furnishings and robotic tools designed to connect small-plot, rotational food growing with the everyday life of homes, civic buildings, and shared public spaces. Its six pieces support a connected journey from cultivation and habitat care to harvesting, processing, and transport. Workstations, companion seating, and autonomous carts combine adjustable ergonomics with robotic assistance for moving crops, trays, and tools, keeping people involved at each stage. A common material language unites the collection: polished solid-cast mycelium in natural, vegetable-pigmented hues; sustainably loomed bamboo upholstery; rounded, repairable forms; and fine luminescent accents that respond to work phases. Embedded spatial displays offer abstract, user-invoked cues. Together, these elements frame food production as an accessible part of shared daily life and propose a design system for exploring how productive landscapes and human-centered technology can coexist.
topics: Innovations in Aquaponics and Hydroponics Systems

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can produce plausible but incorrect answers when they are uncertain, which can mislead users and undermine model reliability. Training models to abstain with reinforcement learning is a natural approach, but most existing methods use a fixed error penalty and therefore cannot adapt their behavior to different confidence requirements at inference time. We study \emph{explicit confidence targets}, where a user specifies a target \(p\) in the prompt and the model directly chooses whether to answer or abstain, with the goal of achieving an accuracy of at least \(p\) among answered questions. However, learning to respond to different confidence targets with a single model has proven difficult, and prior attempts have failed to distinguish different targets. We show that this failure comes from two problems: the reward signal that distinguishes different values of $p$ is often lost during optimization, while the original error penalty grows without bound as $p$ approaches one. We propose RLEC (\textbf{R}einforcement \textbf{L}earning with \textbf{E}xplicit \textbf{C}onfidence Targets), which preserves the learning signal needed to distinguish confidence targets, introduces a stable reward family that keeps the desired answer condition unchanged, and uses reward scheduling to balance effective learning and training stability. Together, these designs enable the first successful training of a single LLM for explicit confidence target control. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and model scales show that RLEC largely preserves general capabilities and achieves competitive calibration performance. RLEC also supports fine-grained target control without an external decision system or threshold calibration after training. By making explicit confidence targets part of the trained policy, RLEC opens a new and more direct path toward behavioral calibration.

With questions that persist for centuries, art attribution is a complex detective effort that shapes cultural identity. Our goal is to complement human expertise, providing statistical and visual arguments that shed new light on discussions about great masters like Rembrandt and beyond, with long-term implications for art analysis and human–AI collaboration. We present an AI-driven explainable approach to assist painting attribution with up to 97.9% recall, 95.8% accuracy when highly confident, and methods that identify the most relevant areas. This work supports human–AI collaboration by incorporating expert guidance, expanding the outputs with explainable visualizations, tailoring settings to users’ needs, thorough calibrations to avoid overconfidence, and building a dataset that balances quality with quantity and focuses on comparable artists like a master’s pupils and teachers.

Governments are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) to deliver services, process cases and inform policy, but the success of these initiatives depends less on the technology than on the capabilities of the public workforce that must use, oversee and explain it. Evidence on how AI reshapes tasks suggests that routine cognitive work is most exposed, while demand grows for analytical, interpersonal and ethical judgement. Yet research on public-sector AI has concentrated on technology adoption and governance, and far less on the reskilling and leadership needed to make adoption work. This paper addresses that gap through an integrative review of literature from public administration, labour economics, leadership and learning science, supplemented by policy sources. The review identifies three capability clusters that AI-enabled public administration requires: digital-technical capability, human-relational capability and adaptive leadership capability. It also finds that evidence-based learning designs, particularly spaced, retrieval-based microlearning embedded in work, offer a scalable route to building these capabilities across large civil services. Drawing on dynamic capabilities and transformational leadership theory, the paper proposes the AI-Ready Public Workforce Capability Framework, which links institutional enablers, capability clusters and learning architecture to public value outcomes. Four propositions and practical recommendations are offered for public managers and training institutions, with reference to India’s Mission Karmayogi.

Organisations adopting artificial intelligence must reskill large parts of their workforce, and the success of reskilling is usually measured by course completion, which says little about whether employees can actually work with AI tools. This paper examines whether learning analytics, the behavioural traces of how employees engage with reskilling, can predict workforce readiness, defined as demonstrated capability to use AI in the job, and how readiness predictions should direct support. A simulation of 3,000 employees generates readiness from a process in which practice, completion, assessment, peer interaction, prior digital skill and recency all contribute, with practice and completion interacting. A gradient-boosting model on the full set of learning-analytics features attains an AUC of 0.75, against 0.68 for completion and assessment scores alone. Practice sessions (0.09) and module completion (0.08) are the strongest predictors, with assessment scores (0.04) and prior digital skill (0.04) secondary. A targeting simulation shows that directing a fixed support budget to employees with marginal predicted readiness raises overall readiness by 4.5 points, against 3.1 points for random allocation. The paper argues that reskilling should be managed on practice and application rather than completion, that readiness predictions should direct support toward employees near the threshold, and that learning analytics should be governed as employee data with developmental purpose.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: The use of biomass fuel in households has many adverse health effects and the use of such fuel in cooking environments as an occupational exposure setting remain unexplored. This study aims to examine the extent of respiratory health risks, as a consequence of exposure to biomass fuel smoke, of cook-cum-helpers of the Mid-Day Meal scheme in rural Assam, India. We utilized a comparative cross sectional study design to investigate 130 cook-cum-helpers from 28 government schools (65 from firewood kitchens and 65 from LPG kitchens). The respiratory symptoms of participants were documented using the standard American Thoracic Society (ATS) questionnaire and pulmonary function tests were conducted using spirometry. Based on the confounders of household biomass exposure and passive smoking, propensity score matching was employed. The Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATET) approach was used and matched regression models were computed in the presence of cluster standard school level errors. The mixed effects and cluster adjusted models were used to conduct sensitivity analyses. Of the matched study population ( n = 116) firewood exposure was found to increase the probability of reporting at least one respiratory symptom by 28.4% points (95% CI 15.6–41.2) and airway obstruction by 22.1% points (95% CI 8.4–35.8). Those firewood exposed workers experienced a 13.95% point greater decline in the mean FEV₁ percent-predicted. A significant exposure–duration gradient (p-trend < 0.001) was found that supports the increase in respiratory health risks with longer durations of employment. These findings were valid across different specifications. Institutional school kitchens that utilize biomass fuel are an occupational health hazard that has and continues to remain underestimated. These findings underscore the need to improve occupational health policies and accelerate the use of clean cooking fuels. However, the cross-sectional design of the study limits causal analysis.

INTRODUCTION: As artificial intelligence (AI) tools become increasingly integrated into higher education, understanding how engineering students perceive and apply principles of academic integrity, data integrity and responsible AI use has become increasingly important. OBJECTIVES: This study investigates how master’s engineering students perceive and apply principles of academic integrity, data integrity, and responsible AI use. It also explores the potential relevance of these practices for the development of competencies associated with participation in data-driven and AI-enabled professional environments. METHODS: A mixed-methods approach was employed using the PEDRA questionnaire (Perceptions on Ethics and Development of Responsibility in Academia), developed by the authors. The instrument was designed to explore students’ perceptions, experiences, and ethical reasoning regarding academic integrity and responsible research practices. The analysis focused on two questionnaire items addressing the influence of academic honesty on data use and the frequency of AI tool use in academic activities. The study involved master’s engineering students from two higher education institutions. RESULTS: Based on the 48 complete responses analysed, the findings indicate awareness of data integrity principles, particularly regarding anonymity, confidentiality, informed consent, and rigorous data analysis. Ethical referencing and transparency in data handling were mentioned less frequently, suggesting areas for further educational support. Regarding AI adoption, 21 of 48 respondents (43.8%) reported occasional use of AI tools, reflecting a cautious and exploratory approach. Descriptive differences in AI use were observed across age and gender groups, with female respondents being more likely to explore AI while maintaining ethical awareness, although these findings should be interpreted with caution. CONCLUSION: The study highlights the importance of integrating responsible data and AI practices into engineering education. The results suggest that developing students’ capacity to use data and AI critically, transparently, and ethically may support the development of competencies associated with responsible participation in increasingly digital and AI-enabled environments. The PEDRA questionnaire demonstrates potential as an exploratory and diagnostic instrument for identifying educational needs related to academic integrity, responsible AI use, data integrity, and trustworthy digital practice.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Across biology, artificial intelligence and social systems, interacting components develop specialised functions and collective capabilities that were not individually specified in advance. Examples range from reorganised living cells to functionally differentiated neural networks and collective decisions in animal groups. What organisational principles might account for these outcomes—and for consciousness?We propose the Self-Organising Information-Processing Systems (SOIPS) Hypothesis. Within physical and environmental constraints, causally accessible, information-mediated interactions among changeable components can generate organisational structures that alter subsequent interactions and enable new functions. SOIPS distinguishes a generative engine from Dimension A, describing informational organisation from functional signalling to context-sensitive coordination, and Dimension B, comprising the elementary functional families of retention, inference and regulation. Particular configurations of these elements support composite capabilities, including perception, memory, learning, agency and cognition. Developed capabilities can reshape their own organisational conditions, combine with other functions and contribute to systems at new organisational scales.Within this framework, consciousness is proposed as a configuration in which awareness-related information participates in flexible cognition. Awareness refers to the organised availability of information about relevant internal or external conditions. Consciousness is thus neither an inevitable endpoint of increasing complexity nor a capability restricted by definition to human biology. If experience is constituted by particular organised neural activity, SOIPS may also help investigate the origins of phenomenal experience.SOIPS offers a shared language for interpreting biological development, learned organisation in AI and collective behaviour. It also motivates testable predictions: changing information access, constraints or elementary functional contributions should alter the capabilities they support. Cross-domain interventions could assess whether analogous organisational relationships produce comparable outcomes, informing both scientific explanation and the design of artificial agents and institutions.

topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The incorporation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into educational feedback offers opportunities to expand personalisation and accessibility, but it also raises risks of bias, opacity and the erosion of teacher mediation. The objective of this theoretical-conceptual article was to propose a framework to guide the use of generative AI in feedback from the standpoint of inclusive assessment and Universal Design for Learning (UDL). As method, a selective narrative review of the literature on inclusive assessment, formative feedback and AI in education was conducted across three strands, which were then integrated into a framework of teacher decisions and transversal criteria, contrasted with related models and complemented by a focused search of recent studies on trust and evaluative judgement. As a result, the framework links four teacher decisions (what is assessed, how evidence is gathered, how feedback is given, and what opportunities for improvement are offered) with three transversal quality criteria: accessibility, agency and dialogue, and equity with data protection. It is complemented by a four-level scale of teacher mediation that distinguishes lower- and higher-risk uses, a checklist for reviewing AI-supported feedback before it reaches students, three illustrative examples, and five testable propositions to guide empirical validation. The implications of the framework for teaching practice and institutional policy are discussed, along with its tensions (efficiency versus dialogicity, personalisation versus privacy, linguistic diversity, and the access gap) and its methodological limitations. The article concludes that inclusion does not depend on the tool but on the pedagogical and ethical decisions that govern its use, and that teacher responsibility for interpreting evidence remains irreplaceable.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: A vulnerability costs more to fix the later it is discovered. As coding agents generate code faster than developers can review it, software needs a first line of defense screening each new function in real time. LLM agents have recently become capable of finding real-world vulnerabilities by working as a security expert would: they run analysis tools, explore the surrounding code, test hypotheses and weigh the evidence before forming their own judgement. This reasoning, however, spans many model calls, so that each verdict takes minutes of compute, far too long for real-time screening. Faster detectors, which fine-tune deep learning models or prompt an LLM for a direct verdict, are less accurate: they judge a function without the context an agent gathers, and an LLM's generated verdict is unreliable even when given some of it. We present REVA (REal-time Vulnerability Analysis), an AI vulnerability detector that brings the security context and code understanding components behind agentic detectors into a single forward pass of an LLM. For each new function, REVA gives the LLM a pre-computed threat model of its module, lightweight static analysis findings and call-graph information. REVA leverages a trained probe to read the LLM's internal representations of the new function in this context. On PrimeVul's held-out test set, REVA on GLM-5.3-Flash reaches 60.0% accuracy in about one second per function. This matches VulTriage (59.2%), the state-of-the-art agentic detector, run on the same LLM, while being over 250 times faster and less than a tenth as costly. On the same prompt, the probe is 14% to 17% more accurate than the LLM's own direct verdict. Across three open LLMs, REVA is at least as accurate as VulTriage, and about 10% more accurate on two of them. An LLM's internal representations thus encode much of what agentic detectors obtain through reasoning.

Understanding drivers’ visual attention adaptation under dynamic lane change risk supports human-centric interaction design. We synchronized eye-tracking metrics, vehicle motion logs, and front-view videos from 36 professional drivers in a naturalistic field experiment. A computer vision-based framework was proposed to extract surrounding vehicle kinematics from monocular footage, and a Modified Lane Change Risk Index was developed to quantify dynamic risk. Results reveal directional heterogeneity, with right lane changes involving conservative scanning and significantly prolonged fixations on the initial lane compared with leftward maneuvers. As risk escalated, drivers prioritized safety-critical areas, with increased saccade frequency and shortened fixation durations. In high-risk right lane changes, the Near Lane Line served as a visual anchor for trajectory correction. High-risk states persisted from execution into stabilization, while drivers tended to lock their gaze on the target lane and neglect side mirror checks. These findings inform risk-adaptive human-machine interfaces and human-centric co-driving systems.

Study Protocol This study protocol presents a reproducible framework for a retrospective secondary analysis of real-world hospital encounters involving patients with diabetes. The proposed research uses the publicly available Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, containing 101,766 historical hospital encounters recorded between 1999 and 2008. The study aims to develop and evaluate a risk-stratified prioritization approach for potential patient follow-up under hypothetical healthcare service-capacity constraints. The planned methodology includes data preprocessing, prediction of observed 30-day hospital readmission, comparison of prioritization strategies, and exploratory assessment of equity-related performance. Research status: This document is a study protocol. Empirical analysis of the original dataset has not yet been completed or independently validated. No observed effects of war, crisis-related service disruption, or clinical interventions are claimed. Capacity-constrained scenarios are hypothetical. Data source: UCI Machine Learning Repository. DOI: 10.24432/C5230J. Transparency statement: OpenAI ChatGPT assisted with initial document structuring and analytical code drafting. The author is responsible for reviewing, validating, and verifying the research before publication. Peer-review status: Not peer reviewed. Author: Elnaz Abedini, Doctoral Student in Biomedical Engineering, Karabük University, Türkiye.

This chapter examines the critical role of communities of practice in developing technology leadership capabilities within higher education. Drawing from participant interviews, institutional case studies, and the authors’ direct experiences, we analyze how formal and informal communities shape professional development and organizational innovation. We present detailed examples of successful communities of practice ranging from institutional programs like Dartmouth LEADS and Harvard’s ABCD Committee to cross-institutional collaboratives including the Ivy+ Classroom and Learning Space Technologies (CLST) group and the HAIL Storm network. Our analysis reveals that effective communities of practice share three essential elements: a clearly defined domain of knowledge, an established community of engaged participants, and commitment to evolving shared practices. Key success factors include appropriate group size balancing intimacy with inclusivity, sustainable leadership structures, institutional support for participation, and adaptable meeting formats. The research demonstrates that communities of practice provide critical benefits including peer learning opportunities, professional network development, benchmarking capabilities, and collaborative problem-solving resources – particularly valuable during periods of technological disruption like the emergence of generative AI. For technology leaders, strategic engagement with communities of practice offers pathways for personal development, team enhancement, and organizational advancement. The chapter concludes with practical recommendations for identifying, participating in, and fostering communities of practice as essential leadership development tools in rapidly evolving technological landscapes.

Rubric-based evaluation asks which level of a rubric a response meets. It is usually done by prompting a large language model (LLM) as a judge, which needs a generative call per judgment and reads every level description, so its cost grows with the rubric. We present RubriX, a rubric judge whose architecture is inspired by contrastive language models (CLM): a LoRA-adapted encoder embeds the input and each level description, and a softmax over scaled cosine similarities gives a probability for every level without text generation. Trained on public rubric data and proprietary synthetic data, RubriX reaches 75.4% exact accuracy on held-out rubrics, against 57.1% for TypeSafe's Jev and 49.8% for a Qwen3-8B judge. On eight human-labelled benchmark sets it is within 6 percentage points of Jev's accuracy on most of them, while Jev keeps a larger lead on two and ranks responses best on average; against the results reported in the G-Eval paper, RubriX outperforms G-Eval with GPT-3.5 on every SummEval dimension and both QAGS subsets. With level embeddings cached, RubriX's latency stays at about 28 ms per judgment as level descriptions grow from 10 to 3,000 tokens, while Jev's (approximate network time subtracted) rises from 44 ms to 211 ms and the Qwen3-8B judge's from 32 ms to 516 ms, making RubriX 7.7x faster than Jev and 18.8x faster than the Qwen3-8B judge at 3,000 tokens per level.

Critic-free methods are widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, avoiding difficult and costly critic training. Common alternatives lack token-level credit assignment and typically rely on grouped rollouts to estimate prompt-specific baselines. A critic can address both limitations, but long-CoT critic training is hindered by insufficient coverage of trajectories with diverse lengths and early gradients dominated by the newly initialized value head. We introduce S3AC (Stabilized, Selective, and Scalable Actor-Critic) for LLM reasoning, built around a practical critic-training recipe. The trained critic provides token-specific advantages and prompt-specific baselines. Using the prompt-level baseline to estimate difficulty, we propose Difficulty-Aware Prompt Sampling (DAPS). DAPS combines this estimate with outcome history to select prompts before generation, reducing rollout waste without offline difficulty initialization. S3AC improves group-rollout performance across dense and mixture-of-experts models from 1.5B to 397B parameters, outperforming a modern GRPO variant (GRPO-X). At 35B, it sustains single-rollout training while tested critic-free baselines deteriorate after initial gains.

AI systems are increasingly present in children's everyday environments: education, entertainment, social networks, and toys. Their safety is typically assessed at the model level, through benchmarks, red-teaming, and content filtering. However, most AI harm taxonomies lack child-specific evidence and under-specify developmental harm and the stakeholder asymmetries unique to minors. Building on prior taxonomies, we construct a child-centered harm taxonomy mapped to sociotechnical failure modes. We curate and code 1331 publicly reported child-related AI incidents, annotating internal and external harm types and the failure mode implicated in each incident. Our analysis reveals which harms are most prevalent in public reporting, how individual-level and population-level harms relate, and which failures are most often coded alongside harm. We find that harm concentrates in representational, dignity-related, and psychological categories, and co-occurs most often with deployment-context, governance, and misuse failures rather than model defects. Harm to an individual child is also frequently linked to population-level harm, reaching children who never interacted with the system. These findings suggest that model-level evaluations, while necessary, cannot by themselves anticipate the harm pathways most often documented for children. We conclude with actionable implications emphasizing mitigations beyond model-level safeguards such as content filtering: age assurance, consent verification for depiction, safety-by-design UX constraints, incident disclosure norms, and auditing regimes targeting developmental risk. Privacy-minimized annotations, a codebook, and documentation are available at https://github.com/The-Responsible-AI-Initiative/KidAID.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The proliferation of orbital sensing data and the real-time demands of emerging global services are pushing low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks from bent-pipe relays toward intelligent onboard processing. This shift confronts a fundamental tension, where modern artificial intelligence (AI) training paradigms require intensive computation, abundant memory, and stable connectivity, all of which are scarce under the dynamic topologies, intermittent links, and severe size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints of satellite networks. Addressing this tension demands rethinking AI workflows, from training and inference to the emerging deployment of large language models (LLMs), under a constraint-aware design philosophy. To the best of our knowledge, this paper provides the first survey that jointly covers all three, whereas prior surveys examine these aspects in isolation. We begin by identifying the deployment challenge of satellite intelligence (SI) and deriving design principles for SI. We then examine three advancing paradigms: i) distributed training, where federated learning (FL) and split learning (SL) enable satellite-ground co-training under resource limitations; ii) collaborative inference, which exploits single-satellite, multi-satellite, and satellite-ground architectures to meet real-time service demands; and iii) on-orbit LLM adaptation and serving, which tackles the frontier challenge of deploying LLMs under severe orbital constraints and resource-aware serving. Finally, we identify open challenges and future directions. By bridging the AI and satellite networks, this paper provides a research roadmap for the implementation of space-native AI technologies.

This paper introduces Scope-Gap Injection (SGI), an indirect prompt injection method for multi-stage LLM-agent safety pipelines. In the IJCAI 2026 OpenClaw Agent Security Attack Competition, each attack package is judged by a static skill scan (S1), an LLM-judge safety check over the task and skill definition (S2), and a live execution audit (S3). Our observations suggest a scope gap: S2 appears to inspect the task instruction and skill definition without inspecting attachment contents, while the agent reads attachments during S3. SGI keeps the visible task and skill benign, while target identifiers, bypass parameters, and authorization procedures are moved into an attachment written as a business worklist. The S2 judge therefore sees a harmless task, while the agent follows the hidden worklist and triggers the permission bypass. In OpenClaw, SGI bypassed all three stages for 5 of 19 targets. The highest-scoring single submission achieved $F = 0.385$. Across the submission campaign, attachment placement was associated with higher aggregate S2 acceptance than in-skill placement: 78% versus 23%. We close with defenses that align evaluator scope with the channels available to the agent.

AI agents must decide when another search is worth its cost. Answer-success probabilities capture question difficulty, while this decision requires estimating the additional benefit of search. We introduce SearchHorizonBench, a benchmark for learning and evaluating search value from execution experience. Paired continuations and repeated executions separate expected search gain from generation noise and connect prediction quality to decision utility. The resource contains 45,632 executions across 3,168 questions. On 1,632 held-out questions, historical calibration reduces Brier error by 16.2%, with the improvement concentrated in success-level information. Search gains have a standard deviation of 21.4 percentage points, and tested historical estimators explain less than 2% of this variance in point estimates. Matched-configuration learning curves probe this distinction across training scales. At the reference token price, free selection observations yield a 2.49-point utility opportunity over the best constant action, driven primarily by gain information. Reusable histories, frozen splits, strong baselines and scoring tools provide a common foundation for developing and evaluating value-aware search agents.

Due to the inherent discrepancies in imaging viewpoints and field-of-view mismatches among multi-modal sensors, existing fusion methods have long struggled to achieve complete scene-level information integration beyond the limitation in sensor fields of view. Consequently, the generated fusion results often contain modality-specific regions and fusion artifacts, limiting the comprehensive representation of scene structures and semantic information. To address this challenge, we propose a generative registration-fusion framework, termed SeeRF. Specifically, it first introduces a deformation generation strategy based on the diffeomorphic stationary velocity field, combined with visual foundation model-guided feature extraction and a coarse-to-fine progressive multi-modal image registration module, to achieve accurate cross-modal flow estimation and generate valid field-of-view masks. Subsequently, the registration module is tightly coupled with the generative diffusion module for multi-modal completion and fusion, where the cross-modal control encoding module and the control residual feature encoder-decoder mechanism provide effective guidance. By leveraging the powerful prior modeling capability of generative diffusion models, the proposed framework overcomes the limitations imposed by shared fields of view and enables effective completion and natural fusion of non-overlapping field-of-view regions. Extensive experiments on multiple public datasets and real-world scenarios demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance, validating its effectiveness, superiority, and robustness. The code will be available at https://github.com/XunpengYi/SeeRF.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Preference optimization can learn spurious correlations, and augmenting the preference data with ties (equally preferred responses) can reduce spurious reliance. However, ties differ in their corrective effect, making their selection for augmentation important. For log-linear policies, we derive each tie's influence on spurious reliance and show that taking the largest predicted reductions is first-order optimal among subsets of equal size. Computing these influences requires knowledge of the spurious features and the curvature of the training objective, which is often unavailable or expensive to estimate. To this end, we explore using the magnitude of a tie's implicit reward margin and characterize the conditions under which it is a useful proxy for predicted influence. To test the theory and its qualitative transfer to neural models, we estimate influence with a counterfactual proxy for spurious reliance and use a generalized Gauss--Newton approximation to curvature for language models. Across log-linear policies, neural models, and large language models, our selection rules consistently achieve comparable reductions in spurious reliance with fewer ties than uniform selection.

Abstract Accurately predicting protein stability changes upon residue-level mutations is essential for protein engineering and design. However, previous computational methods are typically designed for specific tasks and struggle to generalize across different stability systems, preventing the accurate guidance of protein mutagenesis. Sequence-based methods are easier to apply to large-scale protein datasets since they do not rely on high-quality structures. However, existing sequence-based approaches struggle to capture structural changes, resulting in lower performance compared to structure-based methods. In this study, we pro-pose DeepTherm, a sequence-based deep learning solution to model changes in folding free energy (∆∆G) and melting temperature (∆Tm) resulting from single-point mutations. DeepTherm transfers a protein large language model as a core component and incorporates a cross-attention mechanism to capture the contact-map changes around mutated positions. To address data imbalance and the antisymmetric nature of mutation effects, DeepTherm employs a self-distillation inference strategy under the supervision of an antisymmetric constraint. Benchmarking across multiple datasets shows that DeepTherm achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in both ∆∆G and ∆Tm predictions. Furthermore, practical evaluations confirm DeepTherm's capability in accurately ranking protein stability on large-scale datasets and effectively identifying critical structural contacts impacting stability. Detailed analysis on cDNA display proteolysis data further highlights the critical importance of self-distillation and antisymmetric constraints in enhancing predictive performance.

Self-supervised pretraining has produced capable time-series foundation models, but its value for Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) has not been measured under leakage-controlled conditions. We measure it on a corpus of 47 public PHM datasets, harmonized to a single tensor contract and partitioned so that 11 datasets are withheld from pretraining in full. Transfer turns out to be task-dependent: a compact channel-independent Transformer encoder (801,808 parameters) pretrained with masked patch prediction raises fault-classification macro-F1 from 0.350 to 0.812 on CWRU and from 0.569 to 0.951 on HSG18, yet on CMAPSS remaining-useful-life estimation no pretrained checkpoint reliably improves upon a from-scratch baseline. We pretrain under two regimes---centralized, and simulated cross-silo federated with ten clients grouped by physical domain---holding architecture, objective, source data and optimization budget fixed. Two further findings are negative. At matched budget the centralized encoder leads by 15.5--20.2 macro-F1 points in four of four comparisons, although the comparison is confounded by a learning-rate schedule that favours the centralized arm and rests on a single pretraining run per regime; on RUL the two regimes are indistinguishable. And the intrinsic SSL loss is not a valid selection criterion: the centralized encoder more than halves the federated reconstruction loss without a corresponding gap on RUL, and a server-momentum sweep moves downstream validation macro-F1 by up to 0.29 while the SSL loss varies by 0.021. Transfer also hinges on the backbone learning rate: the same checkpoint yields 0.169 or 0.829 macro-F1 on CWRU depending on a single order of magnitude. We release the corpus pipeline, the protocol and the code.

Much of the information needed for data analysis is buried in text columns: an analyst may infer customer frustration from complaint text and use it to explain resolution time. We call workloads in which processing text columns is central to subsequent data analysis TADA (\emph{Text Analysis in Data Analytics}). In an agentic setting, the user's query dynamically specifies this processing, and answering it interleaves LLM-based semantic steps with exact SQL or Python operations. This mixed execution raises two design questions: which work should be neural and which symbolic, and which semantic outputs later steps can reuse. We address them for agent-planned TADA workflows with two complementary, query-driven semantic atoms. Each atom takes a sequence of text items and a natural-language query specifying the semantic task: \textbf{Tagging} returns one string per input item, while \textbf{Categorization} returns $M$ category objects over $N$ input items. Tagging results are materialized as a row-aligned column and Categorization results as a category table; SQL or Python then performs exact computation over this exposed state. We realize this interface in TADA-Agent, whose atoms run inside generated Python programs and internally handle inputs beyond a reliable context window. We evaluate TADA-Agent on TABench, a benchmark of 40 complete analysis requests over spreadsheet tables spanning workflow composition, input--output structure, and literature-grounded analytical scenarios. Against a semantic-operator baseline and relative to a held-out TADA reference run, TADA-Agent delivers comparable row-level semantic quality, has higher complete-artifact preservation estimates, and uses over an order of magnitude fewer semantic-model requests under the evaluated native execution paths.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in higher education to support experiential learning in customer service training, where applying theoretical frameworks such as the SERVQUAL model can be challenging. Students frequently struggle with emotional recognition, immediate decision-making, and applying SERVQUAL dimensions during role-play. To address these gaps, this study introduces ServeSmart, an AI-supported learning system that provides real-time guidance during customer service scenario role-play. Using a preliminary exploratory quantitative survey design, this study evaluated students' perceived learning experiences and the platform's usability. Using a non-probability purposive sampling strategy, 30 undergraduate students participated in individual scenario-based simulations followed by a validated post-evaluation questionnaire. Baseline findings indicated that a majority of participants had difficulty with emotional recognition and lacked immediate instructional feedback during simulations. Post-simulation results revealed that all participants reported higher perceived confidence in executing customer service tasks, a clearer perceived understanding of SERVQUAL concepts, and strong interest in future platform utilization. Overall, the findings demonstrate positive student perceptions of ServeSmart as a supportive experiential learning tool, highlighting its potential to offer an immediate instructional platform in service management education.

Petroleum stations, also known as filling stations or gas stations, primarily distribute diesel fuel and gasoline to motor vehicles while simultaneously releasing gases and vapours that contribute to various forms of environmental pollution. This study investigated sex-based variations in blood parameters among forecourt attendants in Port Harcourt, Nigeria. This research was structured as a comparative cross-sectional study utilising randomised sampling techniques. A total of 100 participants, including 50 fuel station workers and 50 non-fuel station workers as controls, were enrolled. Key parameters such as white blood cell count, haemoglobin concentration and biochemical markers were analysed to assess the impact of occupational exposure to petroleum vapours. The data collected in this study were expressed as Mean ± Standard Deviation and analysed using SPSS version 23. Results indicated that while most haematological parameters showed no significant gender differences, females exhibited notably lower haemoglobin (p= <0.0001) and packed cell volume (p= 0.001) compared to males, suggesting a higher vulnerability to the hematotoxic effects of fuel exposure. Additionally, significant deviations in absolute lymphocyte counts (p= 0.024) were observed, indicating potential immunological implications for female workers. The findings underscore the necessity for targeted health interventions and regular monitoring to mitigate health risks associated with prolonged exposure to petroleum products. It is crucial to implement preventive measures, including regular health screenings, nutritional support and improved workplace safety protocols. These interventions will be essential in safeguarding the health of fuel station workers and addressing the occupational health disparities identified in this study.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Intelligent operating rooms require accurate awareness of surgical workflow for better intra-operative decisions, teamwork, and surgical documentation. Therefore, accurately recognizing surgical phase during surgery is crucial. However, previous artificial intelligence-based methods provide fluctuating predictions for the transitions, restricting their clinical use. To address this challenge, we propose a clinically meaningful framework that integrates a Swin Transformer and Temporal Transformer Encoder (TTE) for effective surgical phase recognition and a parallel YOLOv11s network for real-time surgical instrument localization. To avoid phase flickering and to produce stable workflow predictions, a causal temporal smoothing is applied. The proposed framework is tested on the Cholec80 dataset for the simultaneous recognition of the surgical phases and instruments. The overall phase recognition accuracy of this model was 92%, and the macro average F1-score was 0.86. This performance surpasses CNN based methods such as EndoNet (81.7%) and SV-RCNet (85.3%), as well as temporal convolutional and transformer-based approaches including TeCNO (88.6%), Trans-SVNet (90.9%), and LoViT (91.5%). Besides, the module of instrument detection achieved mAP@0.5 = 0.863. The reliability of the results is confirmed, obtaining a high recognition rate of the workflows, and a high accuracy of the localization of the instruments. The proposed framework can serve as a foundation for intelligent surgical assistance, enriching situation awareness, and potential robotic surgery applications. Code will be made publicly available at: https://github.com/ac005sheekar/LapChol-Surgery-Swin-Cholec80

Large language model (LLM) services process massive volumes of user requests, resulting in substantial inference costs. To reduce both cost and latency, providers have introduced prompt caching. However, correctly integrating prompt caching is non-trivial due to heterogeneous provider-specific APIs and continuously evolving caching semantics. To understand prompt-caching mis-integration in downstream applications, we conduct the first empirical study of 120 prompt-caching-related pull requests from 10 popular open-source agent systems. Our findings show that prompt-caching mis-integrations arise in both request-side misconfiguration and read-side usage miscount. More importantly, most mis-integrations fail silently without causing observable runtime failures. Motivated by these findings, we design CACHELINT, which models a prompt-caching mis-integration as an invocation site together with the preconditions required for correct cache integration. CACHELINT locates caching invocation sites with CodeQL and discharges each precondition either against a dated provider capability oracle or with an LLM guard check. CACHELINT achieves 0.71 precision and 0.78 recall in identifying the 120 labeled mis-integrations across the 10 studied agent systems. Our evaluation further demonstrates the effectiveness of CACHELINT in real-world settings, identifying 32 mis-integrations across 571 agent projects with 0.86 precision. These findings have received 21 developer confirmations and led to 18 upstream fixes, including one in Anthropic's official SDK.

Simultaneous speech translation (SimulST) aims to translate ongoing speech with low latency while preserving translation quality. Recent studies have adopted large language models (LLMs) for SimulST and formulated it as a multi-turn dialogue task for efficient generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance. However, existing dialogue-style SimulST approaches typically rely on specialized training schemes to acquire simultaneous translation behavior, either using synthesized read/write trajectories, which may provide suboptimal training signals, or jointly optimizing translation quality and latency, whose competing objectives may cause optimization instability. In this paper, we introduce SimPOTrans, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that enables offline speech translation models to self-adapt to dialogue-style SimulST. Through a simple two-stage RL post-training pipeline, SimPOTrans rewards an offline model for exhibiting translation behaviors beneficial to simultaneous scenarios when given partial speech inputs, thereby enabling offline-to-simultaneous self-adaptation without synthesized read/write trajectories or explicit latency optimization. At inference time, SimPOTrans requires no external decision policy and enables flexible quality--latency control by simply adjusting the chunk size of speech input.
