Experiments on the ACL 60/60 and MCIF benchmarks across three language directions (En$\rightarrow$De, En$\rightarrow$Zh, and En$\rightarrow$Ja) demonstrate that SimPOTrans outperforms several strong baselines, achieving a superior quality--latency trade-off.

Skills provide LLM agents with reusable procedural knowledge, making appropriate skill selection essential for reliable agent behavior. As skill libraries expand, distinguishing semantically similar candidates becomes increasingly difficult. Existing methods encode or rewrite skill descriptions for relevance-based ranking, yet heterogeneous descriptions can obscure capability differences. To address this challenge, we propose SKALOS, a graph-native reranker that compares skills via explicit capability evidence. Its multi-hierarchy graph aligns equivalent expressions across skills while preserving skill-specific capability evidence. Since individually relevant capability elements may not jointly support a query, semiring-based capability witness learning scores each branch by its weakest evidence, checks joint support for the extracted requirements within one implementation, and selects the strongest alternative. To reduce the influence of extraction errors, we develop ranking-feedback graph calibration that adjusts unreliable evidence for candidate comparison. Experiments on SkillRet show that SKALOS improves NDCG@10 by 2.68 percentage points over a matched text-only reranker. Witness-guided skill selection also increases ALFWorld task success rate from 22% to 29%.

The most common and fatal type of cancer worldwide is skin cancer. Prompt treatment and improved patient results rely on the prompt finding and accurate labeling of skin lesions. As deep learning and artificial intelligence progress, automated diagnostic systems have demonstrated encouraging outcomes, especially when developed using extensive dermatological images. This chapter proposed CNN architecture for skin lesions classification utilizing the HAM10000 (“Human Against Machine with 10000 training images”) dataset. 10,015 dermatoscopic pictures collected from diverse demographics and imaging modalities are included in the HAM10000 collection. It includes seven clinically important categories of pigmented skin lesions: Melanocytic nevi (nv): harmless mole-like growths, Melanoma (mel): a severe and aggressive type of skin cancer, Benign keratosis-like lesions (bkl): which comprise seborrheic keratoses and solar lentigines, The most common types of skin cancer are basal cell carcinoma (bcc), actinic keratoses, and intraepithelial carcinoma (akiec): pre-cancerous and early-stage cancerous lesions, Vascular lesions (vasc): which encompass angiomas and haemorrhages, and Dermatofibroma (df): non-cancerous skin nodules. To enhance model performance and ensure data quality, preprocessing methods like Gaussian filtering followed by Grab-Cut segmentation to extract affected area, and data augmentation are utilized for class imbalance issue. The Proposed CNN used to extract the feature; finally soft max classifier is used to classify 7 types of skin disease with validation accuracy of 98.67. This chapter also highlight various CNN Architecture and discuss challenges in recent skin disease classification.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming paediatric dentistry by supporting dentists in diagnosis, treatment planning, behaviour management, and patient education. AI-based technologies such as machine learning and deep learning enable accurate interpretation of dental images, early detection of caries, prediction of eruption patterns, and identification of developmental anomalies. In addition, AI powered mobile applications, virtual assistants, and chatbots improve communication, reduce dental anxiety, and enhance oral health education among children and parents. These digital tools help personalise care while reducing clinical workload and improving efficiency. This review highlights the evolution of AI in paediatric dentistry, its key applications across behavioural management, diagnostics, forensic identification, and patient communication, as well as its benefits, challenges, and future potential in improving child centred dental care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Cybersecurity is increasingly recognised as a complex adaptive socio-technical system in which security outcomes emerge from the interactions of attackers, defenders, users, organisations, regulators, and autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents. These interactions generate adaptive feedback loops, strategic behaviour, information diffusion, and network effects that drive the evolution of cyber threats and defences. Consequently, phenomena such as attack propagation, cyber-risk contagion, cascading failures, and systemic resilience cannot be fully understood through static or purely technical perspectives. Although evolutionary game theory (EGT), complex systems science, network science, behavioural research, and cyber economics have each provided valuable insights, the literature remains fragmented, with no unified perspective for explaining cybersecurity as an evolving socio-technical ecosystem. This review develops the concept of Social Physics of Cybersecurity as an interdisciplinary perspective that brings these approaches together with human-AI interaction to explain how collective security outcomes emerge from adaptive interactions within interconnected cyber ecosystems. We synthesise research on attacker-defender co-evolution, finite and structured population dynamics, cyber contagion, critical transitions, systemic cyber risk, and the growing role of AI-enabled multi-agent systems. Building on these perspectives, we propose a unified multilevel view of cybersecurity that links individual strategic behaviour, network-level interactions, and system-wide resilience. We argue that cybersecurity should be understood as a social-physical phenomenon in which resilience and vulnerability emerge from the collective dynamics of interacting human and artificial agents. Finally, we identify key research opportunities for developing empirically grounded, data-driven, and AI-enabled models capable of predicting, analysing, and governing increasingly interconnected and autonomous cyber ecosystems.

Individuals with intellectual disabilities face entrenched systemic and cultural barriers to sexual expression, often exacerbated in Chinese contexts by values of ‘face’ and ‘familism’. While artificial intelligence and humanoid sex robots emerge as potential interventions, their ethical and practical viability within disability services remains contested. This study employed Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis to explore the perspectives of 12 Chinese social workers regarding the integration of AI-powered intimate technologies. Findings reveal four major themes: systemic barriers to romantic agency, the perceived benefits of ‘risk-free’ simulated intimacy, ethical concerns regarding relational authenticity, and societal reflections on the ‘eternal child’ syndrome. Practitioners recognised robots as tools to bypass parental opposition and institutional liability by eliminating risks of pregnancy and exploitation. However, a critical tension emerged: whether these technologies genuinely empower users or serve as a ‘techno-fix’ to hide disabled sexuality from the neurotypical public. The results highlight a ‘double standard of readiness’, where cognitive competence is used to gatekeep human rights. We argue for a multidisciplinary governance framework that prioritises ‘techno-social’ literacy and challenges the sexual ableism inherent in current service models.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma

Sovereign artificial intelligence has moved from a legal debate about data residency to a practical question of agency across the whole computational value chain: energy, connectivity, data centres, compute, data, models, applications, skills and governance. This paper reviews an AI-generated report that models national compute ecosystems through infrastructure economics, low-precision arithmetic, game theory and Monte Carlo risk analysis, and augments it into a verified academic treatment. Each empirical claim in the source was checked against institutional sources. Several were confirmed: the scale of the CNAS Sovereign AI Index, the UK Council for Science and Technology's definition of sovereignty as agency, the European AI Gigafactories call and its deadline changes, Bangladesh's draft National AI Policy 2026–2030, the OECD's 2026 due diligence guidance and the specifications of current rack-scale systems. Others were corrected, notably the infrastructure share of projects and the temporary nature of a mid-2026 suspension of foreign access to frontier models; unverifiable figures were removed. The augmentation adds three computed analyses. A synthetic quantisation experiment shows why block-scaled 4-bit formats are central to doing more with scarce national compute. A corrected analysis of the source's openness model shows that its optimum is a single planner's choice, not a Nash equilibrium, and derives its comparative statics. A Monte Carlo schedule model shows that headline probabilities of infrastructure delay depend entirely on assumed distributions and should be reported with them. The paper closes with implications for capital-constrained states, with Bangladesh as a reference case, framed at the level of strategy and policy.

Many institutions have come to recognize the importance of designing physical and digital learning environments based on what we know about how students learn. While higher education can support active learning anywhere, choice architecture suggests that where we learn has a significant impact on how we learn. This chapter will focus on a 25-year retrospective case analysis of leading change with developing physical and digital learning environments at a research-intensive university, through multiple educational disruptions. Adaptations to these changes are structured using change frameworks from the literature to distill four key areas. First, “developing a collaborative vision, governance, and strategic planning” moved opportunistic events to a structured vision. “Decisions based on pedagogical principles, diversity and inclusion” focused on student success and what research has demonstrated can enable successful learning to guide decisions. “Create comprehensive sustainable support” enables a shift of thinking on emerging technologies to look at pedagogical innovation for the long term. Lastly, a “focus on data driven decision making” avoids anecdotal change to support decisions based on actual evidence. This chapter will look toward the future and how learning environments continue to contribute to future teaching and learning success as we adapt to a new disruption bringing us into the age of artificial intelligence (AI). We conclude with recommendations for leaders and centers for teaching and learning (CTLs) on planning physical and digital learning environments and preparing for the next wave of disruption.

Multi-turn jailbreaks turn dialogue safety into a trace property: a violation may become identifiable only when user intent and assistant behavior are considered across multiple turns. Existing guard models largely classify individual messages or exchanges and return risk scores or labels, without executable safety semantics or a formally checkable decision trail. We present SpecGuard, a training-free, specification-driven framework for monitoring multi-turn LLM interactions. SpecGuard uses a fixed atomic-proposition contract to map natural-language observations into causally scoped, evidence-backed facts, and expresses forbidden interaction patterns as Linear Temporal Logic specifications. Each specification is compiled into a symbolic finite automaton that incrementally consumes the resulting dialogue trace. The same monitoring mechanism supports buffered runtime checking and retrospective auditing, while accepting runs produce replayable witnesses that identify the triggered specification, supporting facts, and relevant dialogue turns. Experiments on multi-turn safety benchmarks show that SpecGuard consistently outperforms representative open-source guard models while maintaining controlled false-positive rates. These results demonstrate a practical path from heuristic risk classification toward formally specified, verifiable, and auditable LLM safety monitoring, without learned detector parameters or access to the protected model.

Objective To investigate the current status of artificial intelligence (AI) readiness among nursing students and analyze its influencing factors, providing evidence for the cultivation of AI literacy in nursing education. Methods A total of 684 nursing students from two universities in Hubei Province were recruited as study participants. Data were collected using a general demographic questionnaire and the Chinese version of the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students (C-MAIRS-MS). Descriptive statistics, univariate analysis, and multiple linear regression analysis were employed for data processing. Results The overall mean score of AI readiness among nursing students was 3.47 ± 0.31; the cognitive dimension scored the highest (3.57 ± 0.44), while the competency dimension scored the lowest (3.32 ± 0.48). Multiple linear regression analysis revealed that education level, Self-rated academic performance, Student cadre, Innovation and entrepreneurship project, Large language model use frequency, AI course learning, Programming foundation were significant predictors of AI readiness, collectively explaining 33.3% of the total variance (R 2 = 0.333, adjusted R 2 = 0.311, F = 15.030, P < 0.001) Conclusion Nursing students’ AI readiness remains suboptimal with room for improvement. Targeted interventions addressing key predictors are essential to strengthen AI competency among nursing students.

documents.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into Web search, online recommendation, and intelligent decision-making, the third-party plugin ecosystem centered on model customization continues to grow. Among these, Steering Vectors guide model behavior by intervening in internal representations. However, the open plugin ecosystem also introduces new supply-chain security risks: malicious plugins can disguise themselves as having legitimate functionality and covertly manipulate outputs without significantly affecting model performance. Although this risk poses a real threat, the security issues of Steering plugins in the LLM supply-chain ecosystem still lack systematic research. This paper audits eight mainstream open-source Steering plugin libraries and reveals three structural vulnerabilities: insufficient distribution integrity verification, excessive plugin privileges, and missing runtime monitoring, which offers an attack surface for attackers. To investigate this threat, we propose a malicious plugin, IDH. Specifically, IDH designs a norm-gated mutually exclusive routing mechanism and proposes an information-decay inflection point localization method to automatically select the injection layer, thereby simultaneously achieving benign and malicious functions. To counter such threats, we propose a runtime defense framework, by suppressing anomalous activation interventions and orthogonalizing inter-layer trajectory. We evaluate IDH across five mainstream LLMs, using safety-refusal steering as the legitimate functionality and commercial recommendation manipulation as the hijack objective. Experiments covering six brands across three commercial domains demonstrate that IDH achieves an attack success rate (ASR) of up to 97.8% while preserving high refusal rates on harmful requests.

Discipline in memorizing the Qur’an is an important aspect of the tahfiz program because students are required to be consistent in memorizing, reviewing, and maintaining their memorization. In its implementation, students have different levels of motivation, memorization ability, and readiness to submit their memorization. Some students are still reluctant to submit their memorization, lack focus during learning activities, or experience difficulties in maintaining consistency. Therefore, teacher strategies are needed to support students in developing discipline in memorizing the Qur’an. This study aims to describe the strategies applied by teachers to improve discipline in Qur’an memorization among eighth-grade students in the tahfiz program at MTs Assa’adah II Bungah Gresik, the impact of these strategies, and the supporting and inhibiting factors in their implementation. This research employed a qualitative approach with a descriptive research design. Data were collected through observation, interviews, and documentation. The data were analyzed using the interactive model of Miles and Huberman through data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings indicate that teachers applied strategies including setting memorization targets according to students’ abilities, habituating muroja’ah, providing examples, and giving motivation and guidance to students. The strategies had an impact on students’ discipline in maintaining memorization, conducting muroja’ah, managing their time, and achieving memorization targets. Supporting factors included a conducive learning environment, students’ intrinsic motivation, parental support, and teacher guidance and motivation. Inhibiting factors included fluctuating student motivation, differences in memorization abilities, lack of readiness for memorization submission, and distractions during learning activities. These findings indicate that teacher strategies play a role in supporting the development of students’ discipline and consistency in Qur’an memorization.

Language education, particularly English for Academic/Specific Purposes (EAP/ESP), is navigating a period of systemic disruption. The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence, arriving just after the significant upheaval of the COVID-19 pandemic, has once again altered institutional policies and reshaped student needs. This continuous flux leaves many practitioners in a state of constant reactivity. In line with the conference theme, Innovations in Language Education: Advancing Pedagogy, Practice and Research, we argue for a shift away from responding to educational change toward anticipating and influencing it. This paper presents the conceptual framework and insights gleaned from participants in a Futures Workshop conducted at the conference. Drawing on the multidisciplinary field of Futures Studies (FS), the workshop introduced language educators to three foundational foresight methodologies: Metaphors, the Futures Triangle, and Scenario Planning. Contextualised within the English as a Medium of Instruction environment of Hong Kong, the paper outlines the theoretical rationale for applying FS to strategic thinking within language education, details the workshop's design, and presents initial participant perspectives on the field's trajectory. We conclude that equipping educators with Futures Literacy is critical for cultivating teacher agency, enabling us to design and advocate for preferable pedagogical futures.

Errors in scientific code pose a significant risk to the accuracy of research. Yet, formal code review remains uncommon in academia. This is a particular challenge for interdisciplinary fields, such as mental health research, which increasingly rely on computational approaches. This paper presents a pragmatic experience-based framework for code review procedures in mental health research. In order to facilitate practical implementation, it includes a structured checklist for identifying common coding issues, from data handling errors to flawed statistical analyses. We discuss barriers to introducing code review and how to overcome them, revisit best practices from software engineering, and highlight the emerging role of large language models in automating aspects of code review. We argue that, despite perceived costs, code review significantly enhances the reliability of research results and fosters a culture of transparency and continuous learning. Our proposal provides an adaptable model for integrating code review into research workflows, helping mitigate errors before publication and strengthening trust in scientific results.

Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may support independent preparation without necessarily strengthening students’ connections to the classroom. We examined a structured instructional protocol combining AI exploration, confidence reflection, unresolved question generation, and instructor responsiveness. Following baseline assessment, six intact undergraduate class sections at one Chinese university were randomized equally, with three sections and 110 students assigned to each condition. Assessments were conducted in Weeks 1, 6, and 12, and the intervention began in Week 2. Recomputed item means were analyzed using equally weighted section-level contrasts with four degrees of freedom, supplemented by exact randomization tests. At Week 12, the between-condition difference in classroom belonging change was 0.361 (95% CI 0.145 to 0.576; Bonferroni-adjusted p = 0.029). The corresponding differences were 0.282 for emotional engagement, − 0.497 for reactance to teacher guidance, and − 15.24 points for the confidence–performance discrepancy index (CPDI). Exact two-sided randomization p values were 0.100 for all primary contrasts, the minimum attainable with six balanced sections. Exploratory individual-level pathway and effect-modification analyses were treated as hypothesis-generating because only six sections were observed and the pathway estimates were sensitive to measurement timing. Overall, the structured protocol showed promising differences in classroom belonging and related outcomes, but inference remains limited by the small number of randomized sections, parametric model assumptions, and the preliminary discrepancy measure. The findings therefore concern the combined instructional protocol rather than an isolated effect of GenAI or an established psychological mechanism.

Abstract Graduate employability programmes are usually evaluated with self-report measures. We compared a structured human resource development programme supported by generative AI with career guidance matched on topics, duration and facilitator contact. Twelve intact cohorts of graduates seeking education-sector posts in Guangdong, China (N = 186), were allocated as whole units, six per condition, crossed with institution, facilitator and schedule. Blinded experts gave a global rating (0–100) of recruitment-task materials produced on site, under invigilation and without AI, before and after the programme. Ratings were made without a pre-specified rubric, which limits their interpretation. Among 168 participants with post-test data (overall attrition 9.7%), the adjusted difference favoured the AI-supported programme by 5.38 points (95% CI 2.76 to 8.01; d = 0.60) and was stable across eight specifications. Four new self-report scales showed smaller differences (d = 0.12 to 0.29), none significant after Holm correction; each scale could detect only differences of about d = 0.4. The effect on expert ratings exceeded the mean effect on self-report by 0.37 standard deviations (95% CI 0.10 to 0.63). Component analyses were exploratory. The design cannot separate the contribution of AI from structured practice and feedback.

Rapid growth in biomedical literature has increased the need for auditable methods that convert article-level text into structured evidence data. Air pollution is increasingly framed as a modifiable risk factor for cognitive decline and dementia, but publication growth alone does not indicate a structurally diverse evidence base. We aimed to develop and apply a human-validated large language model (LLM)-assisted role-analysis framework based on structured entity extraction to characterize recent air pollution–cognition evidence. Operationally, role-analysis retains pollutant and cognition-related entities as multi-label fields while assigning a single predominant study-level analytical role to each domain. We conducted an abstract-level evidence-structure analysis of PubMed-indexed human original studies published from 1 January 2020 through 22 March 2026. PubMed formed the primary analytic corpus, and Web of Science was used as a supplementary coverage check. A predefined coding schema was used to extract pollutants, cognitive outcomes, study designs, statistical methods, populations, data sources, geographic settings, and analytical roles from titles and abstracts. LLM-assisted screening, extraction, and role coding were constrained by field definitions, conservative coding rules, and consistency checks. Human validation evaluated screening, extraction, and role-coding outputs. Of the 1,061 PubMed records that entered the four-domain eligibility screening, 406 eligible studies were included. In the screening-validation sample ( n = 106), precision was 1.000, recall was 0.881, accuracy was 0.953, F1 score was 0.937, and Cohen’s κ was 0.899. In the structured-extraction and role-coding validation sample ( n = 81), field-level agreement ranged from 0.765 to 1.000; agreement was 0.926 for pollutant roles and 0.901 for cognition roles. The structured evidence dataset showed concentration around particulate matter and gaseous pollutants, older-adult populations, and cognitive outcomes including global cognitive performance, domain-specific cognition, and dementia-related outcomes. Direct pollutant exposure–cognitive outcome analyses dominated the role structure, whereas mediation, effect modification, and alternative role configurations were uncommon. Evidence sparsity reflected overlapping limitations in pollutant characterization, cognitive domain coverage, analytical role diversity, population representation, geographic distribution, and data-source dependence. The post-2020 air pollution–cognition literature is volume-rich but structurally uneven. A human-validated LLM-assisted role-analysis framework can convert biomedical abstracts into auditable evidence data that preserve multi-label study entities together with study-level analytical-role summaries and help distinguish growth in study volume from structural diversity of the evidence base.

documents.abstract: Nutrition science has traditionally focused on dietary intake, nutrient metabolism, physiology, and health outcomes. Although these domains remain fundamental, advancing public health increasingly requires understanding nutrition within the broader systems that shape food production, processing, access, consumption, and environmental sustainability. This Perspective proposes sustainable nutrition as a unifying concept: maintaining nutritional status that supports growth, development, and health across the lifespan while accounting for population needs, context, and the capacity and resilience of food systems. We describe a Nutritional Ecology framework that conceptualizes nutrition as the product of dynamic, reciprocal interactions among human biology, dietary patterns, food systems, and environmental conditions. Agricultural practices affect food quantity, quality, nutrient composition, biodiversity, water resources, greenhouse gas emissions, and ecosystem resilience, while environmental change influences crop productivity, nutrient density, food safety, and nutrition security. Dietary patterns simultaneously affect chronic disease risk and the environmental footprint of food systems. These interdependencies argue against evaluating human health and environmental sustainability in isolation. We therefore call for a transformation toward integrated, systems-based nutrition research that incorporates biological variability, environmental drivers, and system-level interactions. Multidisciplinary collaborations spanning nutrition, food, agricultural, environmental, epidemiologic, computational, systems, and implementation sciences will be essential. Emerging approaches, including systems mapping, network analysis, computational modeling, artificial intelligence, and multiscale data integration, can identify trade-offs and leverage points for intervention. Integrating nutrition, food systems, and environmental science is a scientific necessity for generating evidence across diverse population contexts that supports resilient food systems, effective dietary guidance, improved clinical care, healthier people, and a healthier planet.

Assistive artificial intelligence systems for visually impaired users commonly address mobility and educational accessibility as separate computational tasks, resulting in fragmented architecture, redundant inference, and inefficient use of computational resources. This study presents SUSTAINABLESIGHT, a resource-aware vision–edge AI architecture intended for wearable deployment that integrates navigation perception and mathematical-expression recognition through shared, context-aware execution. The proposed architecture supports navigation (NAV), learning (LEARN), and hybrid (HYBRID) operating modes and employs a mode-aware scheduler to activate only the computational components required by the current task. A reproducible computational evaluation was conducted using public datasets and measured inference traces on a GPU runtime; no physical wearable device was evaluated. For navigation perception, YOLOv8n evaluated on the COCO 2017 validation set achieved a precision of 0.6343, recall of 0.4746, mAP@50 of 0.5188, and mAP@50–95 of 0.3681, with a mean inference latency of 7.24 ms on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU. Mathematical-expression recognition using pix2tex was evaluated on a fixed 500-expression subset of an Im2LaTeX validation dataset; 499 expressions were evaluable, with a mean normalized similarity of 0.5940, median similarity of 0.6394, and median character error rate of 0.4343. The substantially greater computational cost of mathematical recognition motivated adaptive branch activation. In a 1,000-request trace-driven workload, SUSTAINABLESIGHT maintained 100% request coverage while reducing model invocations from 2,000 to 1,098 (45.10%) and mean request latency from 3562.22 ms to 1311.32 ms (63.19%) relative to a fixed unified baseline. Mean-latency reductions of 16.15–81.61% were observed across five workload compositions, and scheduler ablation showed that avoiding unnecessary mathematical-recognition inference accounts for most of the latency improvement. Sustainability is assessed here as computational resource efficiency; device energy consumption and carbon emissions were not measured. These results indicate that SUSTAINABLESIGHT offers a reproducible, resource-aware basis for integrating mobility and STEM-accessibility workloads, while improved mathematical recognition, deployment of wearable edge hardware, and user validation remain important directions for future work.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Abstract Allosteric regulation represents a fundamental mechanism of protein function, yet distinguishing allosteric from orthosteric protein-binding sites remains a persistent computational challenge. While multimodal protein foundation models offer the potential to integrate complementary biological signals, including sequence, structure, functional annotations, and conformational dynamics, their performance determinants in allosteric binding site detection remain poorly understood. We introduce a unified computational framework for profiling multimodal protein foundation models across distinct binding site separability regimes. Rather than evaluating models solely by predictive accuracy, the framework combines systematic modality embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition to characterize how evolutionary, structural, functional, and dynamical information contributes to allosteric site discrimination. Using the OneProt multimodal model, we evaluate two complementary levels of multimodal integration: (a) encoder architectures that differ in the modalities incorporated during pretraining and (b) downstream combinations of pocket, sequence, and text embeddings used for classification. To systematically probe the determinants of model performance, we benchmark these configurations across four assembled data sets of protein complexes representing a spectrum of biological complexity and a range of structural, dynamic, and evolutionary contexts for orthosteric and allosteric binding sites. Through comprehensive embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition, we demonstrate that model performance is governed primarily by intrinsic data set properties rather than architectural complexity, with data set identity accounting for 63.7% of explainable variance. Across the data sets examined, we identify substantial differences not only in overall separability but also in the information accessible from different pretrained representations. Single-modality controls show that high predictive performance does not necessarily imply reliance on the explicitly provided pocket representation: depending on data set composition, substantial discrimination can already be obtained from sequence- or text-based multimodal representations. Within-protein comparisons nevertheless demonstrate that pocket-containing representations retain binding site-specific discriminatory information when protein identity and the associated sequence and text representations are held constant. At the encoder level, structural and molecular dynamics encoders provide the greatest benefit in intermediate and high separability settings. Example-level analysis further shows that combining data sets can reshape which binding sites are preferentially recognized. These findings establish that the success of multimodal foundation models depends critically on alignment between available modalities and the biological signatures that distinguish regulatory classes in each data set.

Abstract Background Large language model (LLM) benchmarking in clinical medicine is increasingly reliant on LLM-based assessment frameworks; in these systems, one AI scores the outputs of another. This practice relies on the assumptions of evaluator neutrality and rubric consistency. These assumptions have not been empirically tested in clinical fields. Objective In this study, we aim to directly examine these assumptions by using the PARM (Planning-Action-Reflection-Memory) framework as a theoretical lens to characterize endovascular device selection and clinical reflective reasoning as a clinical field. Methods We developed a scoring rubric (C1-C6) with 40 clinical vignettes and 6 criteria across 5 endovascular fields (peripheral artery disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm, chronic venous insufficiency, coronary in-stent restenosis [ISR], and cerebrovascular/neuroendovascular; 8 vignettes per field). Four LLMs were evaluated as clinical decision support systems: GPT-4o (M1), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (M2), Gemini 1.5 Pro (M3), and Llama 3.3 70B (M4). Two LLMs served as independent raters with the same evaluation criteria: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (rater 1) and GPT-4o (rater 2). The rater identity was intentionally disclosed; the primary research question concerned rater scoring behavior rather than the absolute performance of the model. Human assessment was intentionally excluded because its inclusion would have shifted the study question from rater disagreement to rater accuracy, a distinct and secondary question. Interrater reliability was measured using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC 2,1) two-way random effects modeling. Results The combined ICC(2,1) was 0.153 (95% CI 0.007‐0.295). In this exploratory study, the low ICC was not distributed randomly: the magnitude of score differences varied across models (M2 Δ=+5, M4 Δ=+31, M1 Δ=−46, and M3 Δ=−158 points). Scoring behavior analysis identified 2 intrinsically consistent but mutually inconsistent criterion-interpretation models. Rater 1’s scores were most consistent with the reasoning quality approach (partial credit to clinical competence independent of vignette context). Rater 2’s scores were most consistent with the context fidelity approach (near-zero scores for wrong vignette responses independent of reasoning quality). Contrary to the self-preference hypothesis, both raters placed the other higher-performing model above their own. Under rater 1, C6 (PARM reflection) was the lowest-scoring criterion across all 4 models, whereas rater 2 showed greater model-dependent variation in C6 scoring. Conclusions AI raters used in LLM-based clinical benchmarking do not behave as interchangeable scoring tools. Their scoring behavior is most consistent with model-specific criterion interpretation patterns that systematically produce different outcomes. The observed low interrater reliability requires interpretation rather than simply being ignored: it reflects structured, direction-specific disagreement concentrated in models with context-tracking failures, not random inconsistency. PARM reflection showed a notable yet evaluator-dependent scoring pattern that warranted further investigation, rather than being interpreted as an evaluator-independent deficit.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes may reduce documentation burden, but little is known about their adoption during enterprise-scale ambulatory rollout. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of 2901 ambulatory clinicians at an integrated academic health system using linked electronic health record and vendor usage data from December 2024 through May 2025. Clinician adoption was defined as any use during the study period, and monthly visit-level uptake as the proportion of eligible ambulatory visits in which the ambient AI scribe was used. Adoption and uptake varied substantially across practice settings, specialties, and clinician types. Clinician-level adoption was highest in community internal medicine (67%), community general pediatrics (69%), and academic neurology (53%), and lowest in academic general surgery (16%), obstetrics and gynecology (18%), and psychiatry (19%). Community attending physicians and advanced practice providers showed marked increases in median visit-level uptake, reaching approximately 80%-90% in some groups by May 2025. Distinct longitudinal patterns included slow and steady adoption, early use followed by discontinuation, transient use, and late adoption. These findings suggest that implementation support and evaluation strategies should be tailored to local practice context rather than applied uniformly across a health system.

documents.abstract: Purpose This research aims to explore how generative AI (GenAI) recommendation modality (text vs voice) influences consumer recommendation adoption and how this effect further interacts with product type (search vs experience), processing fluency and multitasking to shape consumers’ behavioural responses to recommendations. Given that GenAI recommendation systems increasingly support interactive consumer decision-making, the authors examine modality as a key design feature shaping how GenAI-generated recommendations are delivered to consumers. Design/methodology/approach Across five studies, the authors examine how GenAI recommendation modality influences consumers’ recommendation adoption. The preliminary field study uses actual customer interactions in a natural commercial environment to establish the practical relevance of the phenomenon. Study 1 replicates the core modality effect in a controlled Chinese experiment. Study 2 examines the moderating role of product type. Studies 3 and 4 investigate processing fluency and multitasking as the underlying mechanism and boundary condition, using behavioural measures across all studies. Findings The findings demonstrate that GenAI recommendation modality affects consumers’ recommendation adoption, with text-based recommendations outperforming voice-based recommendations. The modality also interacts with product type and this effect is mediated by processing fluency: text-based recommendations elicit stronger behavioural responses for search products, whereas voice-based recommendations are more effective for experience products. Multitasking further moderates this pattern, favouring voice-based recommendations under high cognitive load across product types. Research limitations/implications The findings are based on controlled experimental settings and future work could examine additional contextual or individual-level moderators to enhance external validity. Practical implications Marketers should tailor GenAI recommendation modalities based on product type and anticipated multitasking environments. Text-based interactions are more suitable for detail-oriented search products, whereas voice-based interactions better suit experience products and multitasking contexts. Originality/value This research contributes to the GenAI literature by identifying recommendation modality as a critical yet understudied design feature of GenAI recommendation systems. The findings show that recommendation modality plays a central role in shaping consumer responses to GenAI-generated recommendations and extend processing fluency theory and task–technology fit by integrating product type and multitasking as key boundary conditions.

This paper investigates how situated AI literacy is conceptualised and enacted in complex and heterogeneous ed­ucational environments such as Adult Education Centres in Italy. Qualitative data from semi-structured inter­views with ten headmasters and open-ended responses from forty-five teachers to an online questionnaire were thematically analysed. The findings suggest that headmasters advocate for more than mere technical training, articulating context-sensitive and practice-oriented views of teachers’ professional development in AI literacy. Teachers’ descriptions of their interactions with GenAI illustrate practices of evaluating, adjusting, and modi­fying AI-generated content, suggesting that the development of AI literacy occurs through practices of repair and maintenance in artificial conversations. Therefore, this study suggests participatory action research as a valuable approach for teachers’ professional development in AI literacy to account for their practices while providing them with space and time for critical reflection and practical experimentation with Generative AI in superdiverse educational environments.

Abstract Paediatric heart care is among the most complex, high-risk environments in medicine. Care is delivered by multidisciplinary teams across operating rooms, catheterisation laboratories, cardiac ICUs, and step-down settings, where small failures in communication or coordination may have serious consequences. Although advances in congenital and paediatric cardiac care have improved survival, dysfunctional team dynamics remain an underrecognised contributor to adverse events, inefficiency, clinician distress, and loss of family trust. This review synthesises evidence on how team dysfunction affects outcomes in paediatric heart care, identifies principal forms of dysfunction, and review system-based interventions that may improve team performance and safety. Drawing on literature from paediatric cardiac care, perioperative safety, critical care, interprofessional collaboration, organisational theory, and team science, the review is informed by the Input-Process-Output model, relational coordination, social exchange theory, psychological safety, and high-reliability organisation principles. Common forms of dysfunction include communication failures, hierarchical barriers, unclear role delineation, weak care transitions, and interpersonal conflict. These factors impair shared situational awareness, delay escalation, increase the risk of errors and complications, and affect family trust and clinician well-being. Evidence supports multifaceted strategies including simulation-based team training, structured communication tools, multidisciplinary case review, debriefing, cross-training, conflict-resolution approaches, leadership engagement, and measurement of teamwork processes. Emerging digital tools and artificial intelligence may support situational awareness and information reliability when carefully implemented. Team performance is a central determinant of safety and quality in paediatric heart care. Improving outcomes requires sustained investment in communication, psychological safety, role clarity, mutual respect, and organisational learning.

Trajectory-based confidence estimation has shown promising performance for large language models (LLMs) by leveraging rich signals from their reasoning processes. However, we find that such confidence estimators can degrade substantially after agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL) as it induces substantial shifts in the reasoning trajectories. More importantly, despite these shifts, we uncover a reliability structure that is largely preserved across Base and RL models: $\textbf{more}$ $\textbf{stable}$ $\textbf{trajectories}$ $\textbf{remain}$ $\textbf{more}$ $\textbf{likely}$ $\textbf{to}$ $\textbf{produce}$ $\textbf{correct}$ $\textbf{answers}$. This preserved relationship provides a transferable, label-free reliability signal for post-RL confidence adaptation. Building on this finding, we propose $\textbf{StaR-TTA}$, a stability-guided framework for label-free test-time confidence adaptation. StaR-TTA jointly learns from correctness supervision and stability-derived reliability supervision on labeled Base trajectories, establishing the connection between trajectory stability and answer reliability. At test time, it reuses stability-induced reliability rankings from unlabeled RL trajectories to adapt confidence scores to the shifted trajectory distribution, without requiring target correctness labels. Across four QA benchmarks, StaR-TTA achieves an average AUROC of \(0.721\), with consistent improvements across unseen datasets, model families and scales, and different Agentic RL algorithms.

We replicate the riichi-mahjong track of "Can Large Language Models Master Complex Card Games?" (arXiv:2509.01328) under a drastically smaller budget: models of at most 2B parameters, one 16 GB consumer GPU, about five GPU-days. (1) With matched data and labels, text is the bottleneck: on the same 100k-decision training set, a 2.6M-parameter convolutional board encoder agrees with the strong AI Mortal on 80.6% of test decisions, above every text-prompt LLM we train (best 77.8%), and places better at the table (2.85 over 1,000 games vs. ~3.0 for the LLMs; paired difference at n=100 not significant). Scaled to 1.71M decisions, a 4.9M-parameter Transformer reaches 94.7% agreement, beats the 0.8B LLMs on identical seeds (-0.45 ranks, sign test p=0.005), and is statistically equivalent to parity against three Mortal champions (TOST within 0.10 ranks, p=6e-4); parity against a teacher-opponent is roughly the ceiling of pure imitation. (2) Training toward the teacher raises teacher agreement more than a 2.5x parameter increase does (+2.5 vs. +1.5 points); on human-record agreement both effects are +1.0, and neither is visible at the table. (3) Few-point agreement differences do not resolve into playing strength within a family: +2.5 agreement points coincide with a paired placement difference of +0.02 +/- 0.12 ranks (p=1.0), and +2.0 points at 2B with -0.06 (p=0.37) - both below the ~0.25-rank resolution of 100 paired games. We also document a paper-code mismatch in the original winner filter, reconstruct its two private engine patches, and show that a divide-and-conquer pipeline makes template-generated Japanese rationales 93% sentence-exact (43% without facts). Per Tenhou's terms we release no trained weights - only code, configurations, and evaluation protocols.

This study examined whether target-informed, author-guided large language model (LLM) refinement alters author-reader alignment and comprehension in Chinese texts. Two controlled experiments compared original texts with versions refined by GPT-4 accessed through ChatGPT, Claude 3 Opus, and, in Study 1, Gemini Advanced. Models received author-provided target ratings or answer-key information that was also used for outcome scoring, making the intervention criterion-linked rather than ordinary copyediting. Participants were recruited through Credamo and randomly allocated by the platform to text-version conditions. Study 1 ( N = 572) measured exact-match alignment with authors’ intended emotional-expression ratings and accuracy on 15 author-keyed comprehension items. Recruitment was extended after inspection of initial results; its inferential analyses are therefore exploratory. The GPT-4 condition showed higher emotional-expression alignment than the original-text condition ( p = .002, signed r = .18). Gemini Advanced reduced alignment at the unadjusted level ( p = .010, signed r = − .15) but did not meet the Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.0083; Claude 3 Opus did not differ from original texts. No comprehension differences were detected. Study 2 ( N = 420) measured exact-match alignment on six textually conveyed scholarly attributes and author-keyed comprehension. Neither GPT-4 nor Claude 3 Opus produced detectable differences on either outcome. Results are conditional on the fixed materials, participant samples, prompts, single-output procedure, criterion-linked guidance, and scoring rules and do not establish preservation of all authorial meaning or objective scholarly quality.

Sentiment analysis of financial documents provides insights into market dynamics and investment decision-making. Among various approaches, target-based sentiment analysis (TBSA) is widely studied for its ability to associate sentiment with specific stock entities. However, existing TBSA datasets are limited to a monolingual setting and lack support for low-resource languages, particularly Thai. While encoder-based models and Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely applied in TBSA research, the effects of language setup and retrieval strategies on model performance remain underexplored. To address these gaps, we introduce a bilingual TBSA dataset comprising 10,295 Thai and 10,104 English financial news articles from 2018 to 2023. We describe the data collection, preparation, and annotation process, including investment-specific sentiment guidelines. Building on this dataset, we investigate two key research questions in financial TBSA: (1) how cross-lingual transfer and bilingual fine-tuning affect encoder-based models, and (2) how different in-context learning (ICL) settings influence LLMs. Our findings highlight the importance of language-aware modeling choices for encoder-based systems in financial NLP, with the best weighted F1 scores reaching 0.773 for Thai and 0.691 for English. For LLMs, we observe that performance benefits more from well-designed instructions and domain-specific criteria than from merely increasing the number of examples, with the best weighted F1 scores reaching 0.892 for Thai and 0.767 for English. These insights suggest that prompt quality–especially in terms of clarity, contextual alignment, and feedback-informed selection–is more impactful than quantity, offering practical guidance for designing effective LLM applications in bilingual financial analysis.

Web services increasingly expose backend interfaces that let users delegate tasks to AI agents, which invoke service operations directly without navigating websites. This shift changes how existing Web vulnerabilities can be exploited. We investigate these changes through VELA, an executable benchmark covering 44 vulnerabilities across twelve Web application families. The benchmark preserves vulnerable backends and derives agent-facing interfaces from legitimate workflows. We evaluate three commercial agents across multiple interface configurations, using controlled comparisons to separate interface effects from agent behavior and independent oracles to verify attack outcomes. Our results show that the agent realizes every attack that direct interface invocation realizes in the reference configuration, so exploitability is set mainly by the interface: 91% of vulnerabilities remain exploitable under the reference design. Interface restrictions prevent some attacks by removing required operations or limiting input control, while retention remains high across vulnerability classes. No case-level loss in the reference configuration is attributed to agent refusal or input normalization, and in one case the agent completed an attack by supplying calls the attacker omitted. Across the tested configurations, interface design affects exploitability more than agent choice, moving retention from 39% to 95% against at most 4.5 points across agents, but some restrictive interfaces also limit legitimate workflows. Our study provides a systematic empirical account of how agent-mediated access reshapes existing Web vulnerabilities, grounding future Web architecture design in measured security outcomes and trade-offs between reducing attack exposure and preserving legitimate functionality in agent-facing services.

Code, materials and derived data for the preprint “The analytic multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis: a framework, open tools, and a screening study” (van Allen, 2026). In the screening study, two large language models coded 40 open-access smoking-cessation trial reports for 94 behaviour change techniques under a half-fraction factorial design (32 configurations, 38 runs). Every run was scored against Human Behaviour-Change Project annotations. The project contains the prospective multiverse declaration, the prompts and codebook, the report × code decisions of every run, the reference, the figures, and analysis scripts that reproduce every reported result without new model calls. No report text or quotations are included. The tools and declaration can be adapted to run comparable multiverse studies on other data.

The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the accounting profession by automating routine tasks, improving data accuracy, and enabling more strategic decision-making. This paper, titled The Blessed Accountant: How Artificial Intelligence Reclaims Time, Eliminates Error, and Elevates Strategy, examines the evolving role of AI in modern accounting and its implications for accounting professionals, organizations, and financial management. AI-powered tools can streamline bookkeeping, invoice processing, bank reconciliations, tax compliance, fraud detection, and financial reporting, thereby reducing manual workloads and minimizing the risk of human error. Beyond operational efficiency, AI enables accountants to shift their focus from repetitive transactional activities toward analytical interpretation, strategic planning, risk management, and advisory services. The paper also explores the challenges associated with AI adoption, including data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, implementation costs, technological dependence, and the need for continuous professional development. It emphasizes that AI should be viewed not as a replacement for accountants but as an enabling technology that strengthens professional judgment, ethical responsibility, and value creation. The effective integration of AI into accounting requires a balanced approach that combines technological innovation with human expertise, regulatory compliance, and appropriate governance mechanisms. The study concludes that AI has the potential to redefine accounting as a more efficient, accurate, and strategically oriented profession, provided that its adoption is guided by transparency, accountability, and responsible use. Ultimately, the future of accounting lies in the collaboration between intelligent technologies and skilled professionals, empowering accountants to deliver greater organizational value.

documents.abstract: The Book of Truth: Omega XV presents an interdisciplinary research corpus and executable reference architecture for the systematic examination of existence, distinction, identity, provenance, evidence, consent, artificial intelligence, institutional responsibility, ecological protection, temporal continuity, irreversibility, and recoverability. Developed within the Boundary and Continuity Science research program, the publication investigates how finite information systems can be formally defined, examined, preserved, and extended into evolving systems capable of registering new evidence, detecting relevant changes, reassessing decisions, and maintaining continuity across successive states. The work integrates philosophical and mathematical foundations with computational methods, proposed ethical safeguards, institutional accountability principles, and operational models for rights-preserving decisions. Foundational structure The framework identifies nine foundational families: Ontology and existence. Identity and provenance. Evidence and epistemic verification. Consent, autonomy, and authorization. Artificial intelligence and computational systems. Institutions, governance, and diplomacy. Ecology and protection of living systems. Temporality, irreversibility, and recoverability. Recursive governance and accountability. These foundations are examined through nine operational phases: definition, observation, distinction, authentication, authorization, action, monitoring, repair, and reassessment. Nine-direction expansion The research applies nine analytical directions: inward, outward, upward, downward, lateral, backward, forward, adversarial, and recursive. Omega XV organizes these directions into a five-axis Cartesian examination registry incorporating direction, foundation, operational phase, affected subject, and failure mode. The resulting finite model contains 59,049 structured examination combinations. This enumeration provides an organized examination space and does not constitute 59,049 independently validated scientific or engineering findings. Mathematical and computational architecture The publication develops a distinction between finite structural closure and continuous system evolution. It incorporates 81 foundation specifications, 81 capability specifications, a directional review register, admissibility procedures, reference decision logic, integrity verification, audit records, and a state-transition approach to evidence and recovery. The proposed living-system sequence progresses through capture, attribution, examination, evidence sufficiency or uncertainty, human review, lawful application, monitoring, and correction or reopening. Historical evidence is preserved without automatically being treated as proof of present conditions. Unknown information is not interpreted as affirmative consent or authorization. Generated representations are distinguished from original identities, and copied sources are not automatically considered independent corroboration. Executable reference system The accompanying archive contains Python reference software with a local browser interface, corpus-related functions, decision checks, audit mechanisms, integrity procedures, and optional scholarly research connectors. The research interfaces support opt-in metadata queries through OpenAlex and Crossref. Network operations are disabled by default and require explicit activation. The software is not represented as a production-certified legal, clinical, governmental, autonomous, or continuously operating monitoring system. Six automated local reference tests are recorded as passing. Source continuity and corpus preservation Omega XV preserves the preceding Omega XIV master archive without modifying its contents. Earlier research editions and associated materials remain available through the nested predecessor archive structure. The edition includes a preservation manifest, structured CSV registries, executable scripts, research manuscript, test results, and machine-readable closure certificate. Threshold Non-Circular Separate Final Closure The framework introduces a bounded closure methodology that distinguishes exhaustive examination of a declared finite structure from unsupported claims of universal completeness. A distinction is retained when it materially changes a protected interest, evidence requirement, legitimate authority, timing obligation, accountability condition, remedy, or recoverable successor outcome. Repetitive formulations without a material operational difference are excluded. Closure is reopened when new evidence, counterexamples, failed safeguards, legal changes, consent limitations, overlooked dependencies, or materially different recovery pathways emerge. Limitations The research does not claim to establish complete knowledge of reality, universal mathematical proof, legal enforceability across jurisdictions, production-ready global monitoring, independent real-world effectiveness, or possession of all possible historical and future source materials. Native operating-system installers, comprehensive nested-document indexing, production network validation, independent scientific and legal review, and institutional deployment remain open implementation obligations. Contribution Omega XV provides a preserved finite corpus, an executable reference implementation, an explicit model for evolving evidentiary and operational states, and a structured method for recording both closure and reopening conditions. Its central proposition is that continuity should preserve distinguishable origins, accountable decisions, legitimate authority, and recoverable future possibilities without confusing generated claims with verified knowledge. Research classification: Interdisciplinary research corpus, mathematical and computational reference framework, structured datasets, and experimental software. Validation status: Bounded structural enumeration and local reference testing; independent real-world validation remains open.

This paper proposes an account of apparent temporal passage within an eternalist interpretation of spacetime. The complete person is conceived as a collective of temporally situated experiencing stages, each possessing its own local present. Apparent temporal passage is explained through asymmetric relationships between experience, memory, anticipation and retrospective interpretation, without requiring a moving present or a consciousness travelling through time. A single widening life-funnel represents cumulative experiential history, while distinguishing the continued existence of past experiences from their accessibility through memory. The model is subjected to critical objections concerning subjective continuity, thermodynamics, personal identity and explanatory redundancy. It is offered as a philosophical hypothesis, not as a new physical law. This investigation was developed through sustained human–AI collaboration between John Sendak and ChatGPT (OpenAI, GPT-6), within FLOW RESEARCH STUDIO.

Today rapid convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, blockchain, and other related paradigms is what is facilitating rapid transformation in smart healthcare. This convergence of multiple technologies is being applied to readily address various urgent products of healthcare, such as the need for real-time monitoring of patients, scalable deployment of clinical decision support systems, a secure means of exchanging patient health information, and governance of patient data in a patient-centered manner. The addition of these new multi-technology ecosystems also creates significant new issues that must be taken into consideration, such as security, privacy, interoperability, explainability, latency, compliance with laws such as HIPAA, and sustainability. As such, we have developed a robust convergence framework to integrate AI-driven intelligence, cloud-native scalability, blockchain-enabled trust, along with other technologies, such as federated learning and edge computing. We will outline a layered systems architecture, identify relevant use cases in practical healthcare settings, and provide design guidelines for deploying robust, trustworthy, and scalable smart healthcare systems. Additionally, we will outline several areas of future research in which we need to focus on privacy-preserving learning, interoperable health data standards, verifiable AI, and energy-efficient computing for next-generation healthcare infrastructure.

documents.abstract: This study examines how pedestrian density, lateral distance, and external Human-Machine Interface (eHMI) type influence discomfort and avoidance behavior with autonomous mobile robots (AMRs). A within-subjects virtual reality experiment with 40 participants manipulated three pedestrian density levels, four lateral distances, and three eHMI types (none, cyan, or red projection). Discomfort and discomfort distance were analyzed using generalized linear mixed-effects models. Higher pedestrian density increased perceived discomfort while reducing discomfort distance, whereas narrower lateral distances increased both outcomes. eHMI type influenced perceived discomfort but not discomfort distance, with the red projection producing greater discomfort. Interaction effects revealed a critical spatial threshold around 120 cm, where the influence of pedestrian density on perceived discomfort shifted from amplification to attenuation. This demonstrates a dissociation between affective and behavioral responses, suggesting constraints may prevent pedestrians from acting on discomfort. The findings highlight the need for density-aware navigation and proactive lateral spacing in shared environments.

Background: Negative life events are associated with lower well-being in children, and this association may vary with physical activity and motivational quality. Objectives: This study examined gender differences in negative life events, physical activity, motivation, and well-being and tested whether moderate and vigorous physical activity moderated the association between negative life events and well-being. It further explored whether intrinsic motivation extended this moderating relationship. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 752 children aged 8–14 years (335 boys, 417 girls; mean = 10.36 years) and their parents. Parents reported negative life events and physical activity; children reported well-being and intrinsic motivation. Moderation analyses were conducted separately by gender, alongside formal tests of gender differences. Results: Parents rated negative life events more severe for girls. Girls also reported lower vigorous physical activity, intrinsic motivation, and well-being. Greater event severity was associated with lower well-being in boys and girls. Formal gender differences in moderations were significant for vigorous but not for moderate physical activity. Follow-up gender-stratified analyses showed that, among girls, higher moderate activity was associated with a weaker negative association between event severity and well-being, whereas higher vigorous activity was associated with a stronger negative association. No interactions were observed among boys. The three-way interactions involving intrinsic motivation were non-significant. Conclusion: A statistically significant difference in moderations was observed for vigorous but not for moderate physical activity. Thus, gender-stratified findings for moderate activity should be considered exploratory. Given the cross-sectional design and subjective assessment of physical activity intensity, findings should be interpreted as associative.

documents.abstract: Background: The use of vibrating power hand tools can lead to Hand-Arm Vibration Syndrome (HAVS). Objective: This quasi-experimental research aimed to determine the effectiveness of ergonomic gloves in reducing vibrations from lawn mowers. Methods: The research instruments were questionnaires. Additionally, this study used a hand and arm vibration meter (SVANTEK SV106A) to measure vibration levels. A repeated-measures design with three conditions (without gloves, with cotton gloves, and with ergonomically designed gloves) was employed in 15 participants. Data was analyzed with Repeated-measure ANOVA, and descriptive statistics. Results: Comparison of average daily vibration levels showed that A(8) vibration while using ergonomic gloves ( x̄ = 3.50 m/s 2 ) was less than using cotton gloves ( x̄ = 4.89 m/s 2 ), and bare hands ( x̄ = 5.23 m/s 2 ) had statistically significant differences of p-value = 0.002 and p-value = 0.003, respectively. Notably, despite the reduction achieved with ergonomic gloves, the A(8) vibration exposure (3.50 m/s 2 ) remained above the Exposure Action Value (EAV) of 2.5 m/s 2 , emphasizing the need for supplementary administrative controls. Additionally, 80% of participants indicated a moderate level of satisfaction regarding the ergonomic gloves. Conclusion: This study demonstrated how agriculturalists and workers can utilize this low-cost, anti-vibration glove prototype constructed from cotton gloves stitched with NBR foam. Furthermore, manufacturing companies can utilize the findings of this study to conduct further research on designing affordable and highly accessible anti-vibration gloves.

documents.abstract: This chapter examines how Davidson College transformed an initial massive open online course (MOOC) experiment into a framework for institutional innovation that proved essential during the COVID-19 pandemic and offers a model for navigating artificial intelligence (AI) disruption in higher education. Through three distinct phases – digital learning R&D (2016–2018), the incubator framework (2018–2020), and crisis-tested refinement during COVID-19 (2020) – Davidson evolved from accidental discovery to systematic innovation capacity. This evolution revealed five transferable principles for adaptive institutional change: start with systematic listening, honor “those closest to the work,” design for users rather than designers, treat resistance as valuable feedback, and build learning capacity rather than solution capacity. The Davidson example demonstrates that institutions facing technological disruption benefit more from developing robust learning systems than from predicting specific technological futures. As AI reshapes higher education faster than traditional strategic planning cycles can accommodate, Davidson’s model offers a tested approach for building organizational resilience through continuous experimentation and adaptation. The framework suggests that small liberal arts colleges can maintain their distinctive identity while successfully navigating technological disruption through systematic experimentation.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being adopted in tourism and hospitality education more quickly than the pedagogical guidance needed to use it well. This study developed the GATE Framework, a GenAI-enhanced active learning environment intended to develop tourism communication competency, and examined its appropriateness through expert review. The work comprised two stages within the first research phase. An evidence-informed synthesis established three connected layers: Inputs, Core Process Components, and Outcomes. At the center of the Process Layer is an iterative Explore-Generate-Apply-Reflect cycle, supported by human-AI interaction, authentic tourism tasks, peer and instructor participation, reflection, and adaptive feedback. In the second stage, nine experts in tourism and hospitality, curriculum and instruction, educational technology, AI in education, and active learning then evaluated the framework using an 18-item, five-point scale and four open-ended questions. The overall rating was very high (x̄ = 4.54, S.D. = 0.58), and the five domain means ranged from 4.52 to 4.56. The experts gave their strongest ratings to the framework's theoretical alignment, relevance to tourism communication learning, and suitability for further development. Ratings remained favorable but were lower for the definition of individual roles and the practical sequence of the learning process. In response, the framework was revised to clarify scaffolding and human oversight, strengthen privacy and transparency provisions, and give greater weight to tourism content rooted in local culture. The resulting framework provides the conceptual basis for GATE-SLE, where GenAI assists disciplinary learning without displacing human judgment.

This essay argues that a person who teaches an AI agent their way of working, one correction at a time, builds a copy of themselves, and that whether the copy replaces them or works for them depends on who owns it. Drawing on eight months of the author's own logs, it separates knowledge, which moves into the machine and gets cheaper, from judgment, which decides the next rule the machine needs. It describes a "higher self", a copy that remembers the rules its owner forgets and can argue against them with their own reasons, and the opposite risk of delegating decisions to an agent that has learned nothing from its user. It answers the objection that such teaching trains a replacement, with reference to Taylor, Braverman, Amodei and Altman, and proposes that a person's way of working, written down as rules, should belong to them and travel with them between employers, while the processes, data and clients of a company stay with the company.

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the transformative influence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) on K–12 educational leadership after the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. The rapid adoption of remote learning technologies created a tech-dependent educational environment, accelerating AI integration in both classroom instruction and school administration. As generative AI tools, such as large language models (LLMs) and chatbots, become increasingly accessible, school leaders face new opportunities and challenges in leveraging these tools to support instructional design, data-driven decision-making, and school governance. This chapter explores how AI is reshaping educators’ roles, enabling real-time feedback, streamlining administrative tasks, and personalizing learning experiences, while also requiring ethical oversight, digital literacy, and sustained professional development. Attention is given to the complexities of equity, access, and teacher readiness, emphasizing the need for thoughtful implementation and culturally responsive AI use.
